title: AWS Certified AI Business Strategist (AIB-C01) practice exam
note: Original questions written from the official exam guide and AWS pages; none is a real exam question.

exam.differences: The beta exam has 85 questions and passes at a scaled 700 of 1,000. AWS's own pages give 170 minutes (certification page) and 130 (exam guide). Multiple-response questions on the real exam can have two or more right answers out of five or more options; here they are choose two of five or choose three of six.

domains.name: AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

questions.stem: A regional bank's operations director hears that its loan-default model "learns every time a customer applies." The vendor's documentation says the model was last updated a year ago. Before briefing the board, she wants to describe accurately what happens when an application is scored. Which description is MOST accurate?
options: The algorithm retrains on each application before it returns a score.
The model looks up the applicant in last year's training records.
The trained model uses learned patterns to predict this case.
The model returns a guaranteed outcome from fixed approval rules.
questions.explanation: Machine learning has two phases: training, where the algorithm finds patterns in historical data, and prediction, where the trained model is given new input and predicts an output. Scoring a new application is the second phase, so the model is using what it learned, not learning again.
whyWrong: Training happened earlier on past loans; scoring a new case does not retrain the model.
A model predicts for new, unseen cases rather than looking up stored records.
ML outputs are probabilities learned from data, not guaranteed results from fixed rules.

questions.stem: A logistics firm's COO is reviewing a vendor's demand-forecasting model. The vendor's deck says the forecasts "are always correct once the model is trained." The COO must now set guidance for how planners use the forecasts in weekly ordering, where a large miss means costly excess stock. What is the MOST appropriate guidance?
options: Use forecasts as estimates and keep planners reviewing exceptions.
Let forecasts place orders automatically and remove the planner review step.
Ignore forecasts until the vendor proves a year of perfect accuracy.
Ask the vendor to replace the model with fixed ordering rules.
questions.explanation: Machine learning models are probabilistic: they say there is a certain chance of an outcome, not that it will happen. Planners should use forecasts as strong estimates and keep human review where an error is expensive.
whyWrong: ML forecasts carry a chance of error, so removing all review ignores costly misses.
No ML model is perfectly accurate, so this standard would block any use.
Demand patterns are what ML is suited to, and fixed rules discard that benefit.

questions.stem: A retailer's marketing VP is presenting three proposals to the board: a churn score built from purchase history, a tool that drafts new product descriptions, and a fixed discount rule applied at checkout. A director asks which proposal is generative AI, since that is where a new budget line sits. Which proposal is generative AI?
options: The churn score built from purchase history
The fixed discount rule applied at checkout
All three, as each one uses data to make decisions
The tool that drafts new product descriptions
questions.explanation: Generative AI creates new content such as text, images or audio. Drafting product descriptions creates new text, so it is generative AI. The churn score is predictive ML, and the discount rule is plain rule-based logic.
whyWrong: A churn score predicts from past data; it is machine learning, not content generation.
A fixed rule follows set instructions and does not learn or create content.
Using data to decide does not make a system generative AI.

questions.stem: A hospital network's strategy lead is writing an AI glossary for board members who have mixed technical backgrounds. The draft has several statements about how AI, machine learning and generative AI relate. Inaccurate wording has already caused confusion in budget debates. Which statements should the lead keep? (Choose two.)
options: AI systems learn from data rather than following written rules.
Machine learning is one branch of AI, and not all AI is ML.
Generative AI is a separate field that sits outside machine learning.
Machine learning is the umbrella term, and AI is one branch of it.
Generative AI is a form of deep learning that creates new content.
questions.explanation: AI is the umbrella term, and machine learning is one of its branches, built on algorithms that find patterns in historical data. Machine learning and deep learning fall under AI, and generative AI is an advanced form of deep learning that creates new content.
whyWrong: AI also includes rule-based systems, so not every AI system learns from data.
Generative AI is an advanced form of deep learning, which sits inside machine learning.
AI is the umbrella term, and machine learning is one branch within it.

questions.stem: An insurer's CEO tells investors the company "already uses machine learning" because claims are routed by a long-standing rules engine built on hand-written if-then logic. A board member asks the head of strategy whether that description is accurate before the claim goes into the annual report. What is the BEST answer?
options: Yes, any automated decision system is machine learning.
It can count as AI, but it is not machine learning.
Yes, a rules engine becomes ML once it runs long enough.
No, rule-based systems fall outside AI entirely.
questions.explanation: AI covers many methods, including rule-based systems, while machine learning is the branch that learns from data instead of explicit instructions. A hand-written rules engine can sit under the AI label but is not machine learning, so the claim should be reworded.
whyWrong: Automation alone is not ML; ML learns patterns from data without explicit instructions.
Running for years does not make hand-written rules learn from data.
AWS lists rule-based systems among AI methods, so they can count as AI.

questions.stem: A telecom's customer-experience director holds two data sets: monthly billing tables with account numbers and amounts, and thousands of recorded support calls. She wants to find the most common complaint themes before next quarter's planning. Which data does this goal rely on, and what does that imply for the approach?
options: The structured billing tables, analyzed with standard queries alone
The billing tables, after staff type each call into a table row
The unstructured call recordings, which usually need ML to analyze
Neither, as AI works on data already stored in tables
questions.explanation: Complaint themes live in the audio of support calls, which is unstructured data. Unstructured data is harder to search and typically needs machine learning, such as sentiment analysis, to analyze.
whyWrong: Billing tables hold amounts and IDs, not the complaints described in the calls.
Manual transcription into tables is slow and loses detail ML can analyze directly.
AI and ML are often used precisely on unstructured data such as audio.

questions.stem: A manufacturer's finance lead wants to forecast next quarter's spare-parts demand. The data is years of order records with part numbers, dates, quantities and regions. A vendor is pitching a generative AI chatbot as the answer. Before comparing vendors, what should the lead conclude about the type of AI that fits?
options: A generative model fits best, as it can explain each forecast in words.
Rewriting the order data as free-text documents comes first.
A foundation model reading the order records through RAG fits best.
Patterns in the structured order history point toward traditional ML.
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says use cases that find patterns in complex but pre-defined input data, such as demand forecasting, point to traditional ML. Generative AI fits widely varying natural-language input or creating new content, which this task does not need.
whyWrong: Wording the output does not change the task, which is finding patterns in pre-defined records.
Converting tabular records to text adds work and suits the vendor, not the task.
AWS points pattern-finding in pre-defined data, such as demand forecasting, to traditional ML.

questions.stem: A property-management firm's operations head is building a data inventory for a new AI program. She wants to tag each source as structured or unstructured so the team can plan the right tools and storage. Which sources should she tag as unstructured data? (Choose two.)
options: Scanned lease contracts stored as long documents
A rent ledger with tenant ID, amount and due date
A unit list with floor, size and rent fields
Video footage from building security cameras
A maintenance log with dates and status codes
questions.explanation: Structured data fits a table of rows and columns, such as numbers, short text and dates. Large documents and video do not fit a table, so they are unstructured.
whyWrong: Fixed fields such as IDs, amounts and dates fit a table, so this is structured.
Short fixed fields per record are structured data.
Dates and codes in set columns are structured data.

questions.stem: A lender's chief risk officer reviews a pilot credit model. Accuracy is strong overall but much weaker for applicants under 25, who make up a small share of the training data. The product team wants to launch next month to hit a revenue target. What should the CRO require FIRST?
options: Launch now and track complaints from younger applicants afterward.
Collect more under-25 data and recheck results for each group.
Remove age from the data and keep the launch date.
Present the strong overall accuracy to the board as sufficient.
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says to check whether data represents the full range of expected users and to close gaps by collecting more data from under-represented groups. Results should then be rechecked by group before release.
whyWrong: Waiting for complaints lets known unfair results reach customers.
Dropping a field does not fix the lack of examples for that group.
A good average can hide poor results for an under-represented group.

questions.stem: A retail chain's CFO is reviewing the first-year budget for an enterprise AI program. The draft puts most of the money into model compute and almost nothing into data preparation, integration or governance. The program lead says compute is "where AI costs live." Which change BEST reflects where early AI costs actually fall?
options: Move budget toward data readiness, integration and governance.
Keep the compute share and add data funds later if issues surface.
Buy the largest model available to offset weak data.
Cut the governance line to fund extra compute capacity.
questions.explanation: An AWS finance view of AI spending says compute is typically only 10 to 15 percent of the early investment. The real costs are data readiness, integration, change management and governance, and skipping them causes roadblocks at scale.
whyWrong: Skipping data work early causes roadblocks when the program tries to scale.
A bigger model does not fix poor data and raises costs.
Governance is one of the main early costs, not a spare line.

questions.stem: A utility's customer-service director learns the outage-prediction model performs poorly. A review finds missing meter readings, inconsistent region codes across systems, and noisy sensor values in the training data. The vendor recommends switching to a newer algorithm. What is the MOST effective next step?
options: Adopt the newer algorithm and keep training on the current data.
Retire the model and return to manual outage forecasts.
Lower the accuracy target so the model passes review.
Clean and reconcile the training data, then retrain the model.
questions.explanation: A model's performance depends on the quality of its training data. Missing values, inconsistent entries and noise all lower accuracy, so fixing the data addresses the root cause.
whyWrong: A new algorithm trained on the same flawed data inherits the same problems.
The cause is known and fixable, so abandoning the model is premature.
Moving the goalposts hides the problem instead of solving it.

questions.stem: An HR director at a software firm plans to train a resume-screening model on ten years of past hiring decisions. Over that period, most hires came from a few universities and one demographic group. Recruiters are eager to cut screening time this quarter. What is the MOST likely outcome if the model is trained on this data as it is?
options: It corrects past bias by itself as it finds better candidates.
It sets history aside and scores each resume on merit.
It learns the past hiring pattern and repeats its bias.
It refuses to predict until the data is balanced.
questions.explanation: Models learn from historical data, so they inherit its patterns. AWS notes that if historical data favors a certain demographic, an ML model used in HR may keep favoring it.
whyWrong: A model learns what is in its data; it does not correct bias on its own.
Training on past decisions is exactly how history shapes its scores.
Models do not detect imbalance and stop; they simply learn from it.

questions.stem: A mortgage lender's pricing model was trained when interest rates were low and tested well at launch. Rates have since risen sharply, and analysts see the model's estimates now skewing against some applicant groups. The business owner asks how a model that passed testing can now be off. What is the BEST explanation?
options: Live data now differs from the data the model learned from.
The model was overfit and needs replacing with a rules engine.
Models wear out after a fixed number of predictions.
Analysts are misreading results that have not changed.
questions.explanation: A model learns from the conditions in its training data. When live data moves away from that, such as mortgage rates changing, its outputs can become biased, so bias needs checking after deployment too.
whyWrong: The change follows a shift in real conditions, and rules would not capture rate effects.
Models do not degrade by use count; they drift when the world changes.
The skew follows a real shift in rates, so dismissing it is unsafe.

questions.stem: An insurer's claims VP wants a supervised model that flags likely fraudulent claims, trained on several years of past claims. Before approving funding, she asks the data team what the training plan must include for the model to be credible over time. Which items should she require? (Choose three.)
options: A vendor guarantee in writing that every flagged claim is truly fraud
Past claims labeled with confirmed fraud or genuine outcomes
A training set limited to this year's claims
A separate data set held back to test the model
Removal of human claim reviewers at go-live
A plan to monitor and update the model as patterns change
questions.explanation: Supervised learning needs examples labeled with the right answer, such as fraud or genuine. A separate validation set checks the model generalizes to new data, and ongoing monitoring keeps it relevant over time.
whyWrong: ML gives probabilities, so no vendor can guarantee every flag is right.
Discarding years of labeled history leaves too few examples to learn from.
Flags are predictions with a chance of error, so reviewers are still needed.

questions.stem: A healthcare software company runs its AI features on AWS. Its compliance manager drafts a sales sheet saying the company is ISO/IEC 42001 certified, since AWS holds that certification. The head of governance must approve the sheet before a major customer bid closes. What should the head of governance do?
options: Approve the claim, as the AWS certificate also covers its customers.
Approve the claim once the AWS certificate is downloaded.
Reword the claim to say the company is ISO/IEC 42001 aligned through AWS.
Remove the claim and pursue the company's own certification.
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 42001 sets requirements for an AI management system, and AWS's certificate covers AWS's own AI management process for a stated scope. AWS says customers are not certified by association, though its certification may make the customer's own certification easier.
whyWrong: AWS states customers are not automatically certified by association.
Holding a copy of AWS's certificate does not certify the company.
AWS's certificate covers AWS's own AI management system, not the company's.

questions.stem: A bank's chief risk officer wants one international standard the bank can be externally audited and certified against for how it governs AI across the lifecycle. The board wants a recognized certificate within two years. A consultant shortlists several frameworks. Which should the CRO choose?
options: ISO/IEC 42001, the management system standard for AI
ISO/IEC 22989, which describes AI lifecycle stages
ISO 31000, a general enterprise risk management standard
The NIST AI RMF and its four core functions
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 42001 is the international management system standard for AI and gives a framework for governance across the AI lifecycle. Organizations seeking ISO certification need annual external audits, which fits the board's goal of a recognized certificate.
whyWrong: 22989 describes what an AI system is and its lifecycle; it is not the AI management system standard.
31000 covers enterprise risk in general, not an AI management system.
The NIST AI RMF is a risk framework, not an ISO certification standard.

questions.stem: An airline's finance operations manager wants to automate refunds. The policy is short and exact: a full refund if cancelled 24 hours before departure, otherwise a travel credit. A vendor proposes a generative AI agent to judge each case. Auditors require every refund decision to be traceable. What is the MOST appropriate approach?
options: Let the generative AI agent judge each refund case.
Automate the written refund policy with fixed rules.
Train a custom model on past refund decisions first.
Keep refunds manual until an agent proves itself elsewhere.
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says to check whether a problem can be solved by writing down a clear and compact set of rules, and to choose AI only for clear, substantial benefits. A two-condition refund policy passes that test, and rules are also easy to audit.
whyWrong: The policy fits a few clear rules, so AI adds cost and less auditability.
Training a model for a two-line policy is effort with no clear benefit.
The task can be automated now with simple rules, so waiting wastes effort.

questions.stem: A distributor's procurement head wants to read thousands of supplier emails in varied formats and languages, pull out price changes, and propose replies. The current rules-based parser breaks whenever a supplier changes its wording. The IT team suggests adding more rules. What is the BEST assessment?
options: Keep adding parser rules each time a new supplier format appears.
Replace the parser with robotic process automation alone.
Use AI, as varied wording defeats any compact rule set.
Require suppliers to adopt one template before any change.
questions.explanation: The test for AI is whether a clear and compact set of rules can solve the problem. Varied, changing natural-language emails fail that test, which is where AI provides a clear benefit over rule-based software.
whyWrong: Formats keep changing, so the rule set can never be clear and compact.
RPA follows fixed steps and suits standardized tasks, not varied wording.
Dictating formats to many suppliers is unlikely and delays the benefit.

questions.stem: A public agency's digital director is screening a long list of proposed AI projects. Agency guidance says to verify that AI is actually required before committing funds, and the budget covers only a few projects. Which checks should she apply to every proposal? (Choose two.)
options: Whether a clear, compact set of rules could solve the problem
Whether a peer agency has announced a similar AI project
Whether the vendor offers the newest model available on the market
Whether the team can launch before the budget cycle ends
Whether reliable training and test examples can be obtained
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says to ask whether the problem can be solved by a clear and compact set of rules and whether reliable training and test examples exist. If rules work or data is missing, a non-AI solution or a reframed use case may be better.
whyWrong: Others' plans do not show that AI is needed for this problem.
Model novelty says nothing about whether the problem needs AI.
Speed to launch is a schedule concern, not a test of AI need.

questions.stem: A travel company's product director compares two tools. Tool A answers questions from a fixed script. Tool B takes a goal such as "rebook this family after a cancelled flight," checks options, uses booking systems and hands off to staff when needed. Which capability BEST marks Tool B as an AI agent?
options: It answers customer questions in natural language.
It runs on a schedule set by the operations team.
It returns a single prediction for each input.
It pursues a goal by choosing its own actions.
questions.explanation: An AI agent is given a goal by people and then independently chooses the actions to achieve it, including deciding when to hand off to a human. Natural language alone or a fixed script does not make a tool an agent.
whyWrong: Scripted chatbots also use natural language without acting as agents.
Scheduled execution describes a basic software agent, not goal-driven AI.
Single predictions describe traditional AI such as classifiers.

questions.stem: A bank's operations VP plans to use an AI agent to draft replies to commercial customers' account disputes. Mistakes could cost money and trust, but the business wants replies out faster than today. Legal has not set a zero-error rule for these replies. Which agent deployment approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Human in the loop, with staff reviewing drafts
Fully autonomous, with periodic audits of sampled replies
Human-led, with the agent limited to research support
Fully autonomous first, adding reviewers if complaints rise
questions.explanation: AWS describes four autonomy levels matched to risk. Draft responses are a medium-risk example suited to human in the loop, with regular review and exception handling, which balances speed with control.
whyWrong: Full autonomy suits low-risk tasks such as routing, not costly disputes.
That level is for critical, zero-tolerance work and gives up drafting speed.
Adding oversight after harm is governance bolted on too late.

questions.stem: A logistics firm's COO is evaluating a platform marketed as "agentic AI." She suspects it may be a relabeled chatbot and wants to confirm real agent capabilities before signing a three-year contract. Which capabilities should she look for? (Choose three.)
options: Acts on set goals and plans its own steps
Follows one fixed script in every conversation it handles
Uses tools and systems to carry out actions
Assigns each input it receives to one predefined label
Runs as a scheduled nightly report for managers
Works with other agents and people on shared tasks
questions.explanation: AWS describes AI agents as goal-oriented: people set goals and the agent chooses actions. Agents extend their reach through tool integration and can collaborate with other agents or human agents to complete larger tasks.
whyWrong: Fixed scripts describe rule-bound chatbots, not agents.
Labeling inputs is a traditional classifier task.
A scheduled report does not pursue goals or take actions.

questions.stem: A retailer launched a GenAI shopping assistant six months ago. Launch testing was strong, so the team moved to other projects. Customer satisfaction with the assistant has since slipped, and nobody can say when the decline began or why. What should the product owner have put in place at launch?
options: A second round of testing before go-live
A production baseline with alerts for drift from it
A larger model to delay any decline in answer quality
A yearly review by the original build team
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says to set operating baselines from real production data and use drift detection to flag when performance moves away from them. Without a baseline, no one can tell when or why quality began to slip.
whyWrong: More pre-launch testing cannot detect changes that happen after launch.
A bigger model does not stop drift and still needs monitoring.
A yearly check is too slow to catch a decline when it starts.

questions.stem: An insurer's CFO questions the ongoing operations budget for a GenAI claims assistant that is already in production. "Our payroll software has run unchanged for years," she says. The AI program lead must justify the budget at Friday's review. What is the BEST response?
options: GenAI license fees tend to rise at each contract renewal.
GenAI code needs the build team to fix bugs daily.
GenAI quality can slip as data and user needs change.
Run costs fall away once launch testing has passed.
questions.explanation: Unlike deterministic software, a GenAI application's performance can degrade over time from data drift, concept drift and shifting user expectations. It must be managed as a living system with monitoring and improvement.
whyWrong: Licensing terms vary and do not explain why AI needs active management.
The issue is changing data and expectations, not daily code defects.
Passing launch tests does not stop performance from drifting later.

questions.stem: A food distributor's demand model has run well for a year. Monitoring now shows a rising share of missing values and inconsistent entries in the store data feeding it, though forecasts still look normal. The business owner must decide how to respond. What should the owner do FIRST?
options: Wait until forecast accuracy drops before acting.
Mute the data alerts until the quarterly review.
Swap in a larger model to absorb the noise.
Have the upstream data issues fixed now.
questions.explanation: Monitoring alerts on data quality give owners early warning so they can act, for example by auditing upstream systems, fixing quality issues or retraining. Acting before forecasts degrade is the point of proactive detection.
whyWrong: Early alerts exist to allow action before results degrade.
Silencing alerts removes the early warning monitoring provides.
A larger model does not fix a broken data feed.

questions.stem: A law firm's managing partner learns that associates are pasting client documents into free consumer AI chat sites. IT proposes an immediate firm-wide ban on all generative AI. Associates say the tools save hours each week. What is the MOST effective response?
options: Provide an approved tool and monitor unapproved use.
Ban all generative AI and announce penalties for breaches.
Allow any tool if staff remove client names first.
Wait for regulators to issue rules before acting.
questions.explanation: AWS notes that outright bans lead employees to use consumer-grade tools, creating shadow AI. The recommended dual approach is to provide approved tooling and build observability to detect unauthorized use.
whyWrong: Bans push staff toward consumer tools out of sight of the firm.
Consumer tools may use submitted data, and manual redaction is unreliable.
Client data is leaving now, so waiting leaves the risk open.

questions.stem: A manufacturer's CIO is publishing the company's first AI tool list. Discovery found several high-risk consumer AI tools in daily use. The sanctioned assistant goes live in three weeks. Staff rely on the consumer tools for daily reporting. When should the CIO block the riskiest consumer tools?
options: Today, before any approved alternative exists for staff
Only once the approved alternative is live
After an incident shows data was exposed
Never, as blocking any tool hurts staff trust
questions.explanation: AWS's 30-day plan is to discover, offer an approved option, then block the highest-risk tools only after the approved alternative is live. Employees then have somewhere legitimate to go.
whyWrong: Blocking with no alternative pushes use to personal devices.
Waiting for harm leaves a known risk open.
High-risk tools still need a red line once an option exists.

questions.stem: A hospital's security chief is publishing an AI tool classification. An already approved note-taking app shipped a new AI feature last month that procurement never reviewed. A clinical team also wants a new AI vendor whose security and privacy reviews are not finished. Which actions fit the classification approach? (Choose two.)
options: Treat the app's new AI feature as approved along with the app
Let the clinical team use the new vendor during its review
Review the new AI feature inside the approved app
Leave both off the list until staff ask about them
Mark the new vendor under evaluation until reviews end
questions.explanation: AWS warns that AI features embedded in already approved software become shadow AI, since procurement reviewed the vendor and not the new feature. New vendors go through security, privacy and procurement reviews that take time, so they stay unapproved until those reviews finish.
whyWrong: The original review predates the feature, so it never covered it.
A tool still under review is not approved for use.
Unlisted tools leave staff guessing, which feeds shadow AI.

questions.stem: A consumer brand's marketing manager uses a GenAI tool to write product summaries. Outputs are generic, vary in length and ignore the brand's tone. The manager's prompt is simply "Write a product summary." A vendor is already offering a custom model. What is the MOST effective first fix?
options: Fine-tune a custom model on the brand's past marketing copy.
Switch to the largest model the provider currently offers.
Add instructions, context, an example and an output format.
Switch to a different GenAI product with built-in brand templates.
questions.explanation: A good prompt combines a task instruction, context about the domain, demonstration examples and the input. A one-line prompt gives the model too little to work with, so adding these elements is the cheapest effective fix.
whyWrong: Fine-tuning costs far more and should follow prompt work, not replace it.
A bigger model still gets the same vague request.
A new product given the same one-line prompt will still produce generic copy.

questions.stem: A customer-service director's team tested a new GenAI prompt for drafting refund emails. Some drafts are good, but others miss key policy details. After one round, the team wants to declare prompt engineering a failure and buy a different product. What is the BEST next step?
options: Buy the different product and keep using the same prompt.
Send drafts as is and let customers flag errors.
Stop the project, as AI cannot follow refund policy.
Review failed drafts, refine the prompt and test again.
questions.explanation: Prompt engineering relies on trial and error: you check outputs and keep refining prompts until you get the outcome you need. One mixed round is the normal start of that cycle, not a failure.
whyWrong: A new product with the same prompt likely repeats the problem.
Customers would receive wrong policy details.
One mixed round does not show the task is beyond AI.

questions.stem: A finance shared-services lead pays per token for a GenAI invoice assistant, and costs are well above plan. Each prompt carries long boilerplate, many redundant examples and loose instructions. The lead wants savings without hurting output quality. Which prompt changes should the lead ask for FIRST? (Choose two.)
options: Add several more examples to each prompt to lift quality
Tighten instructions with clear constraints on the output
Move the assistant to the largest model the provider offers
Trim redundant examples and boilerplate from every prompt
Fine-tune a custom model before changing prompts
questions.explanation: A well-scoped prompt with clear constraints gets accurate results in fewer tokens. AWS's finance guidance notes that shorter prompts, fewer examples and tighter instructions add up to real savings without losing quality.
whyWrong: More examples add tokens and cost to every request.
Larger models usually cost more per token.
Fine-tuning is costly and skips the cheaper prompt fix.

questions.stem: A legal operations manager asks a GenAI assistant to review a very long master services agreement in a single request. Answers about clauses near the start of the contract are often vague or wrong, while later clauses are handled well. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The input exceeds what the model can process at once.
The model was trained mostly on short legal documents and memos.
The early clauses are written as unstructured text.
The provider changed the model after the upload.
questions.explanation: AWS notes that for long prompts, some systems consider only a select number of words. Without fully processing the prompt, the model gives irrelevant or wrong answers that look like hallucinations, which fits a contract too long to handle in one request.
whyWrong: Training data does not explain why only early clauses fail.
The whole contract is unstructured, yet later clauses work fine.
Nothing suggests a model change, and it would not target early clauses.

questions.stem: A support-center director runs a GenAI chatbot that resends the same full product manual with every customer message. Volume is high, monthly costs are climbing and replies are slowing. The vendor says nothing can be done without a larger contract. What is the BEST change to recommend?
options: Send the full manual twice to raise accuracy.
Switch to the largest model to speed up replies.
Cache the repeated manual content shared across requests.
Drop the manual and rely on the model's own general training.
questions.explanation: Prompt caching stores frequently reused prompt content, such as large shared context, so repeated queries skip redundant work. AWS says it reduces latency and cost for high-volume, repetitive queries like support bots.
whyWrong: Doubling the input doubles token cost and slows replies further.
Larger models are usually slower and cost more per token.
The model would lose the product facts it needs.

questions.stem: An electronics retailer's support head wants a GenAI assistant to answer questions on return policies and product specs that change every week. A vendor recommends fine-tuning a model on the current policy documents. The head must choose an approach before the holiday season. What is the BEST approach?
options: Fine-tune weekly on the latest policy documents.
Use RAG to pull current documents at answer time.
Train a custom foundation model on the company's data.
Have agents paste every policy into each prompt.
questions.explanation: RAG supplies the model with private or frequently updated data at answer time, without retraining. Fine-tuning suits changing the model's tone, format or task behavior, not keeping up with weekly fact changes.
whyWrong: Fine-tuning changes behavior and is costly to repeat weekly for facts.
A custom model is far more effort than this need justifies.
Manual pasting is error-prone and bloats every request.

questions.stem: A pharmacy chain's communications lead uses RAG so its GenAI assistant answers with correct, current facts. The facts are right, but replies still miss the required tone and fixed layout even after extensive prompt work. The team holds thousands of approved example replies. What should the lead consider next?
options: Add more policy documents to the RAG knowledge source.
Build a fully custom foundation model from scratch.
Drop RAG and rely on prompting alone.
Fine-tune the model on the labeled replies.
questions.explanation: AWS's customization spectrum says to move to fine-tuning when tone, format or task-specific behavior still falls short after prompt engineering and RAG, and thousands of labeled examples exist. That matches this case exactly.
whyWrong: The facts are already correct; the gap is tone and format.
A custom model is far beyond what a tone gap needs.
Removing RAG would lose the correct, current facts.

questions.stem: A wealth-management firm's COO is reviewing a plan to customize a GenAI model that drafts client briefings. The plan jumps straight to the most expensive option. She wants to apply AWS's customization guidance before approving any spend. Which principles should the COO apply? (Choose three.)
options: Start with prompting and move up only when it falls short
Begin with a fully custom model to lock in a long-term advantage
Use RAG when answers need private or frequently updated data
Fine-tune first, as retrieval costs too much to run
Save fine-tuning for tone or format gaps with labeled examples
Skip prompt work whenever the firm has private data
questions.explanation: The customization spectrum says to start with the simplest approach and go deeper only when needed. RAG grounds answers in private or changing data, and fine-tuning fits tone, format or task gaps when thousands of labeled examples exist.
whyWrong: Custom models are the last step and most workloads never need them.
The guidance puts RAG before fine-tuning, not after.
Private data is a reason to add RAG, not to skip prompting.

questions.stem: A regional bank's board has told the head of customer operations to bring in an AI tool this year. Three vendors are already pitching chat assistants, document readers and forecasting models, but the operations team has not agreed which customer problem matters most. What should the head of customer operations do FIRST?
options: Ask each vendor for a live demo using sample data from the bank
Agree which customer problem and outcome matter most to the bank
Choose the assistant with the best reviews among peer banks
Pilot the three tools across the bank's branches at the same time
questions.explanation: AWS CAF for AI guidance says to work backwards from existing business and customer problems and the effect AI can have on them. Only once the problem and desired outcome are agreed can the bank judge which vendor capability fits.
whyWrong: Demos put the technology ahead of an agreed business problem.
Copying peers' choice skips defining the bank's own outcome.
A wide pilot with no target problem scales before anything is proven.

questions.stem: A home-goods retailer's strategy lead is mapping each candidate AI capability to the business outcome it should move, using the outcome types in the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework for AI. One candidate personalizes product and service recommendations for each shopper. Which business outcome should the lead map this capability to?
options: Reducing business risk
Improving ESG performance
Lowering the IT team's infrastructure cost
Growing new and existing revenue
questions.explanation: The AWS CAF for AI lists four outcome types and gives personalized product and service recommendations as its example of growing new and existing revenue. Mapping each capability to the outcome it moves keeps the use-case list tied to business value.
whyWrong: Risk reduction fits uses such as spotting faulty parts, not shopper recommendations.
ESG fits uses such as flagging environmental compliance reports.
Recommendations aim at customer purchases, not internal IT spend.

questions.stem: After a company-wide ideation workshop, a property insurer's transformation lead holds 30 candidate generative AI ideas and budget for one proof of concept this quarter. Engineers favor an idea that showcases a new multimodal model, but its link to any business metric is vague. Which idea should the lead select for the proof of concept?
options: The idea that best showcases the newest multimodal model
The idea that received the most votes from staff at the workshop
The idea tied to a measurable cut in claim handling cost
The idea that needs the least data preparation work
questions.explanation: AWS strategy guidance says to prioritize business value over technological feasibility and pick initiatives that directly move revenue, cost savings, customer satisfaction or another quantifiable measure. The claim-cost idea is the only one with a clear, measurable business link.
whyWrong: Technical novelty is not a business outcome.
Popularity does not show measurable business impact.
Ease alone does not make an idea worth the only funded slot.

questions.stem: A hospital network's operations director must recommend whether to buy a vendor's clinical-notes product, build a solution on a managed foundation model, or engage a partner. The board expects the recommendation within a month. Which factors should carry the MOST weight in the build-buy-partner decision? (Choose three.)
options: Regulatory requirements for handling patient data
Which option uses the newest foundation model available
Total budget and the timeline to go live
Which option a peer hospital network chose last year
In-house skills to build and run the solution
The programming language each option is written in
questions.explanation: The AIB exam guide names budget, timelines, capabilities, vendor proposals and regulatory compliance as the factors in a build-buy-partner decision. Patient-data rules, cost and time, and in-house skills decide which path the network can deliver safely.
whyWrong: Model novelty says nothing about fit, cost or compliance.
A peer's choice reflects its own budget, skills and rules, not this network's.
This is an engineering detail, not a business decision factor.

questions.stem: A logistics company's sales director wants to adopt a third-party enterprise CRM application with built-in generative AI drafting rather than build anything. The legal team is worried about how customer data entered into the tool will be used. Following AWS guidance for off-the-shelf AI applications, what should the director prioritize before signing?
options: Review the enterprise agreement and which data may be shared
Commission detailed threat modeling of the vendor's model internals
Have engineers fine-tune the vendor's model on CRM data
Sign now and check the data terms at contract renewal
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says off-the-shelf AI (Scopes 1 and 2) calls for a buyer's perspective: manage risk through data governance and carefully review enterprise agreements. The director needs to know which data is authorized for sharing and under what terms before committing.
whyWrong: Detailed threat modeling is the builder's view for custom scopes.
Fine-tuning is a builder task and does not answer the data question.
Checking data terms after signing bolts governance on too late.

questions.stem: A mid-size insurer's CIO wants the company's small data team to build a document-intake AI system from scratch. Several mature products for this task already exist in the market, and the team has never shipped a production AI system. What is the MOST appropriate recommendation for the CIO?
options: Build from scratch to keep full control of the design
Hire a large AI team first, then decide what to build
Wait until a competitor has proven that the approach works in production
Assess existing market solutions before committing to a build
questions.explanation: The AWS CAF for AI tells leaders to push back on the not-invented-here syndrome and to check which solutions already exist in the market, and how mature they are, before building. With mature products available and an inexperienced team, buying or partnering should be weighed first.
whyWrong: This is the not-invented-here pattern the guidance warns against.
Hiring before deciding commits cost before the options are known.
Waiting ignores mature solutions that are available now.

questions.stem: A consumer-goods company's AI steering group has 12 proposed generative AI use cases and funding for three proofs of concept. Each sponsor argues that their own idea is the most urgent. Following the AWS generative AI maturity model, how should the steering group decide which three use cases to fund?
options: Fund the three ideas whose sponsors hold the most senior roles
Fund the three ideas that use the newest AI models
Rank them all by feasibility, impact and strategic fit
Split the budget evenly across all twelve proposed use cases
questions.explanation: The AWS generative AI maturity model recommends a use case matrix that prioritizes projects by feasibility, business impact and alignment with strategic goals, then short-lists the top ones for proofs of concept. That gives the group a shared, defensible basis for choosing.
whyWrong: Seniority is not a measure of value or feasibility.
Model novelty is a technology-first criterion.
Spreading thin funds everything and proves nothing.

questions.stem: A retailer has piloted a generative AI tool for product descriptions for six months. Measured results show no conversion lift, and its cost keeps rising. A separate returns-triage pilot is beating its targets and needs more funding to expand. What should the AI portfolio lead do?
options: Lower the description pilot's targets so it can pass review
Stop the description pilot and move its funds to returns triage
Extend both pilots six more months without changes
Expand the description tool across the whole product catalog right now
questions.explanation: AWS strategy guidance says to be ready to pivot or eliminate initiatives that fail to deliver business value and reallocate resources to more promising ones. Six months of measured results justify stopping the description pilot and funding the pilot that is working.
whyWrong: Moving the goalposts hides the lack of value.
Extending a failing pilot with no change keeps it in limbo.
Scaling a pilot with no proven value multiplies the loss.

questions.stem: A utility's AI pilot for predicting equipment failure showed strong value at three plants. Before rollout, the team finds that sensor data is incomplete for half of the remaining plants. Leadership still ranks the use case as a top strategic priority. What is the BEST portfolio decision?
options: Pause the rollout until data for the other plants is fixed
Terminate the initiative and remove it from the AI portfolio
Scale to all plants and fill the data gaps once live
Swap in a larger model to make up for the missing data
questions.explanation: AWS data-strategy guidance says to validate that the data each use case needs is available and suitable before implementation. The value and priority argue against stopping, while the data gap argues against scaling, so pausing is the proportionate call.
whyWrong: Terminating discards a proven, high-priority use case.
Launching without the needed data risks unreliable predictions.
A bigger model is a builder answer and cannot replace missing data.

questions.stem: An insurer's HR director wants a generative AI chatbot so staff can find which of 40 policy documents covers their question. Legal requires staff to read the official policy text itself, not AI-written summaries. The documents are already well titled and tagged by topic. What should the HR director recommend?
options: Deploy the chatbot to answer policy questions in its own words
Fine-tune a model on the 40 policy documents first
Pilot the chatbot with the HR team before deciding
Treat it as a search problem that finds the right file
questions.explanation: AWS responsible AI guidance says to consider reformulating a use case so it can be solved by rule-based systems, traditional information retrieval or other software. Staff here only need to reach the right official document, which a search tool does without generating answers. AI should be chosen only when it gives a clear, substantial benefit.
whyWrong: Generated answers go against legal's rule that staff read the official text.
Tuning a model adds cost for a need that simpler software already meets.
A pilot still assumes generative answers, which legal has ruled out.

questions.stem: A city agency's program manager is screening proposals for AI agents before any funding is approved. She wants to spot proposals where traditional automation, or leaving the work with staff, would serve better than an agent. Which findings MOST suggest an AI agent is a poor fit? (Choose two.)
options: Requests arrive as varied free text that needs interpretation
None of the cases needs context, judgment or adaptation
The task is rare, but a wrong decision is very costly
The task is rare and each case has little business value
Staff spend many hours a week on the task across departments
questions.explanation: AWS agentic AI economics guidance says purely mechanical tasks that need no adaptation may not need agentic intelligence, and asks whether an agent will be cost-effective given its upfront cost and the volume needed to justify it. Low-volume, high-value decisions can still justify agent help, so rarity alone is not the test.
whyWrong: Contextual interpretation is where agents add value over rule-based processing.
Low-volume, high-value decisions can still justify agent help for decision quality.
Heavy effort shows a problem worth solving, not that an agent is wrong for it.

questions.stem: A shipping firm's operations lead wants an AI agent to copy tracking numbers from a fixed-format carrier file into the order system. The task is high volume, follows the same steps every time, and needs no judgment or context. Which approach BEST fits this task?
options: A fully autonomous AI agent that is checked by periodic audits
Traditional automation such as robotic process automation
A co-pilot agent that suggests each entry to staff
A model fine-tuned on past carrier files
questions.explanation: AWS agentic AI economics guidance says highly standardized, simple tasks are better served by traditional automation or robotic process automation. Agents earn their cost on tasks that need reasoning, context or adaptation, which this one does not.
whyWrong: Agents add reasoning the task does not need, at extra cost.
A co-pilot slows a task that needs no human judgment.
Tuning a model is a builder effort for a deterministic copy job.

questions.stem: A travel company's customer-service assistant runs on a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock. The product owner learns that the model has entered its Legacy period, with an end-of-life date about six months away. The assistant handles most customer chats. What should the product owner do FIRST?
options: Wait for AWS to move the assistant to a newer model
Keep using the model until the end-of-life date passes
Plan and test a move to an Active model before end-of-life
Switch to the newest model next week without testing it first
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock says customers should migrate to an Active model before the end-of-life date, because migration does not happen automatically and requests fail afterward. Starting the plan and testing now protects business continuity for a critical assistant.
whyWrong: Bedrock does not migrate workloads automatically.
After end-of-life, requests to the model fail.
An untested switch risks continuity for an assistant that handles most chats.

questions.stem: A health insurer plans to move claims intake from a manual process to an AI-based solution next quarter. The COO asks the program manager which considerations must be planned before the switch. Which THREE should the program manager prioritize? (Choose three.)
options: The programming language used to build the solution
A fallback to the manual process if the AI solution fails
A press release announcing the go-live date
Whether claims data is available and fit for the use case
Removing the manual process on day one to force staff adoption
Running costs of the new solution against today's process
questions.explanation: The AIB exam guide lists business continuity, cost implications, data readiness and performance impact as key considerations when moving a process onto AI. A fallback, data readiness and a cost comparison cover three of them.
whyWrong: This is an engineering detail, not a transition consideration.
Publicity does not protect continuity, cost or quality.
Removing the fallback puts business continuity at risk.

questions.stem: A media company plans to switch its article-summary feature from its current foundation model to a cheaper one. Finance wants the change live next week to capture the savings, and readers rely on the summaries daily. What should the product lead require before the switch goes live?
options: Re-run the quality evaluation on the new model
Switch at once and wait for reader complaints
Ask finance to fund the current model instead
Retrain the new model on the full article archive
questions.explanation: AWS responsible AI guidance says to re-run the evaluation for each system update and record which version produced which results. A model swap is a system update, so quality must be checked before readers see it.
whyWrong: Waiting for complaints lets readers find the quality problems.
This avoids the decision rather than managing the change.
Retraining is a builder task and skips checking quality first.

questions.stem: An airline's contact-center director reports that the new generative AI assistant has 99.9% uptime and answers in under two seconds. The CFO asks whether the assistant is worth renewing next year. Which KPI should the director add to the report to answer the CFO?
options: Average response time per request
Number of prompts sent each day
Share of the assistant's servers running at peak load each day
Change in cost per resolved customer contact
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says every technical metric should trace to a meaningful business outcome, and an ROI dashboard should combine cost per interaction with business value. Cost per resolved contact speaks directly to the renewal decision.
whyWrong: Response time is a technical metric with no business result attached.
Prompt volume measures activity, not value.
Server load is an infrastructure measure, not a business outcome.

questions.stem: A software company's HR director is defining KPIs for an AI assistant that answers employee policy questions. She wants the scorecard to show tangible and intangible benefits separately so leadership sees the full picture. Which TWO KPIs measure intangible benefits? (Choose two.)
options: Satisfaction of employees using the assistant
Reduction in HR contractor spending
Revenue from a new HR product offering sold to clients
Lower cost per policy question answered
Productivity of the HR advisers
questions.explanation: The AIB exam guide gives cost reduction and revenue growth as tangible benefits, and customer satisfaction and employee productivity as intangible ones. Satisfaction and adviser productivity are real gains that are harder to put a direct financial number on.
whyWrong: A spending cut is a tangible cost-reduction benefit.
Revenue growth is a tangible benefit.
Unit cost reduction is a tangible benefit.

questions.stem: A bank's strategy office is drafting success measures for a multi-year AI program. The CEO wants to include only results that can be measured this quarter, but several goals, such as deeper customer relationships, will take years to show. What should the strategy office recommend?
options: Use quarterly cost savings as the main success measure
Pair quarterly measures with goals tracked over years
Track long-term vision goals, reviewed by the board each year
Set the success measures after the first program year
questions.explanation: The AWS CAF for AI says an adoption strategy should rest on tangible, short-term measurable impact or at least aspirational, longer-term impact, and should factor in both. A mix keeps near-term proof while still tracking the multi-year goals.
whyWrong: One near-term measure drops the long-term impact the program is meant to deliver.
Vision goals alone give no near-term evidence of progress.
Defining success late leaves the first year unmeasured.

questions.stem: A logistics firm will roll out an AI tool that drafts customs declarations next month. The operations VP must later prove to the board that the tool cut processing time. Nobody currently records how long each declaration takes to prepare. What should the VP do FIRST?
options: Roll out now and survey staff about time saved later
Use the vendor's published time-savings figures as the baseline
Measure today's processing time per declaration before rollout
Track how many declarations the tool drafts each day
questions.explanation: AWS guidance on measuring AI results starts with a baseline measurement of the process before AI touches it. Without that before number, the VP has nothing to compare the after number against.
whyWrong: Recalled estimates after launch cannot prove the change.
Vendor figures do not describe this firm's process.
Usage counts do not show whether processing time fell.

questions.stem: A publisher's COO is reviewing a proposal for an AI project that speeds up report production. The proposal records a baseline of five hours per report, but it names no target and no person responsible for the business result. What should the COO require before approving the project?
options: A target outcome and an owner accountable for the result
A larger budget for the AI model and its supporting infrastructure
An engineer named as owner of the deployment date
A plan to define success once the tool is live
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says measuring AI results needs a baseline, a clear definition of the targeted outcome, and an owner accountable for the business result rather than the deployment. The proposal has only the first of the three.
whyWrong: More budget does not define what success looks like.
Owning the deployment is not owning the business result.
Defining success after launch makes the result unprovable.

questions.stem: A software firm gave its developers an AI coding assistant three months ago and only now wants to show the tool's effect on delivery. Detailed ticket records from the year before the rollout are still available. What is the BEST way for the engineering director to set the baseline?
options: Ask developers to estimate their speed before the tool
Use the first month after rollout as the baseline
Skip the baseline and report usage of the assistant
Use pre-rollout ticket records as the baseline
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says a measurement framework starts with baseline metrics using historical data where available. Pre-rollout ticket records give a true before picture, which survey recall or post-rollout data cannot.
whyWrong: Memory-based estimates are unreliable and easy to bias.
Post-rollout data already includes the tool's effect.
Usage shows adoption, not the effect on delivery.

questions.stem: A retailer's finance partner is building the total cost of ownership for a customer-facing assistant built on Amazon Bedrock. The first draft counts only the model usage charges. Which THREE indirect costs should the finance partner add to the AI cost? (Choose three.)
options: Vector database storage used for retrieval
Per-token charges for the foundation model
Marketing spend for an unrelated seasonal product launch campaign
Data transfer between the assistant and other systems
Monitoring, reporting and dashboard licenses
Seat licenses the retailer already pays for its email system
questions.explanation: AWS cost guidance says AI total cost of ownership adds indirect costs to direct service charges: storage including vector databases, data transfer, monitoring and reporting, and agentic calls. Leaving these out understates the cost side of the ROI.
whyWrong: This is a direct cost the first draft already counts.
Unrelated marketing is not a cost of this assistant.
An existing email cost is not caused by the assistant.

questions.stem: A software company's FinOps lead reports that each bug fixed with AI help now costs about $500 in AI spend. An executive presents this figure to the board as the project's ROI. What is the MOST accurate response from the FinOps lead?
options: The figure is the project's full ROI and needs no further analysis
Cost per outcome is a building block for ROI, not ROI itself
ROI is the change in total cloud spending
ROI cannot be worked out for internal productivity tools
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says cost per outcome is AI cost divided by a business value metric, and is the unit-level building block for ROI, not ROI. ROI comes from relating that cost to the value the outcome delivers.
whyWrong: It leaves out what each fixed bug is worth to the business.
Cloud spend alone ignores the business value side.
AWS guidance shows how to tie internal AI to value metrics.

questions.stem: An underwriting team's AI tool cut file review time by more than half. A year later, the CFO sees no change in revenue, cost or volume and asks why the original ROI case has not paid off. What is the MOST likely gap in how the ROI was framed?
options: Review accuracy was checked too often during the year
The tool was billed on a consumption basis
Nobody committed to turning saved hours into results
The model chosen was too small for file reviews
questions.explanation: AWS research found that nearly half of the interviews describing efficiency gains had no evidence of business impact, and that saved capacity is likely absorbed unless someone commits to producing a result from it. Time savings belong in an ROI case only with that commitment.
whyWrong: Checking quality does not stop savings from turning into results.
The pricing model does not explain the missing business impact.
The time saving shows the model did its job.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company launched an AI research assistant to 400 scientists two weeks ago. The executive sponsor wants an early read on whether the initiative is on track, long before any research cost savings can be counted. Which measure gives the BEST early signal?
options: Repeat usage and task completion among the scientists
Yearly reduction in research cost per approved compound
Revenue from products the assistant helped develop
Total compute capacity provisioned for the assistant
questions.explanation: AWS guidance tracks user engagement, such as active users, repeat usage and task completion, as part of business health, and notes that delivered value depends on user adoption. These signals show up within weeks, while savings and revenue confirm results much later.
whyWrong: Cost results arrive long after launch and confirm value late.
Revenue is a lagging result that takes years to appear.
Capacity shows spend, not whether the tool is working.

questions.stem: A manufacturer's board is reviewing a planned agentic AI program before approving the next funding stage. Directors want early evidence that the program is likely to deliver value at scale. Based on AWS research into the gap between AI ambition and execution, which TWO findings are the strongest predictors of success? (Choose two.)
options: A large first-year budget announced to investors
Strong enthusiasm for AI among senior leaders
Measurable success metrics agreed before work begins
Many vendors actively pitching agentic AI products to the firm
Data architecture judged well equipped for the agents
questions.explanation: The AWS and HBR research names data readiness as a root cause of the gap between AI ambition and results, and finds that missing success metrics leave executives with blind spots. It advises setting measurable objectives before you begin, so agreed metrics and ready data are early signs of a program that can deliver.
whyWrong: Spending plans signal ambition, not readiness.
Enthusiasm is common and does not close the execution gap.
Vendor interest says nothing about internal readiness.

questions.stem: Two AI pilots at an insurer have similar early accuracy. Pilot A has an executive sponsor, a dedicated team and a funded plan for running the system after launch. Pilot B is run by volunteers in spare time with no budget past the pilot. Which conclusion is MOST justified?
options: Both pilots are equally likely to succeed
Pilot B is more likely to succeed with its lower cost
Neither pilot can be judged until revenue results arrive
Pilot A is more likely to reach and stay in production
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says lasting success needs executive sponsorship, dedicated teams and resource planning, and that promising projects can stall mid-implementation without it. Pilot A shows those early signals and Pilot B does not.
whyWrong: Equal accuracy ignores the resourcing that predicts success.
Low cost with no budget past the pilot often stalls.
Waiting for revenue ignores the early signals available now.

questions.stem: A bank's compliance team uses a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock to summarize thousands of archived documents each night. Nobody reads the summaries until the next morning, and on-demand charges are growing fast. Which change BEST lowers cost without hurting the business result?
options: Switch the job to a larger, more capable model
Move the nightly job to batch inference
Buy seat-based licenses for each compliance officer
Run the summaries in real time throughout the day
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock offers batch inference for select models at a 50% lower price than on-demand. Work that nobody needs instantly, like overnight summaries, is a natural fit for batch.
whyWrong: A larger model usually costs more per request.
Seat licenses do not reduce model usage charges.
Real-time processing costs more and is not needed here.

questions.stem: An online retailer's AI spend tripled after it launched a customer-support assistant. Every request goes to the largest available model, and monthly usage still swings widely as features change. Finance proposes a three-year fixed-quantity contract to cap the bill. Which actions should the product owner recommend? (Choose two.)
options: Sign the three-year fixed-quantity contract sized for peak use
Route simple requests to smaller, lower-cost models
Move the traffic to a newer model of the same size
Stay on pay-as-you-go pricing that tracks actual use
Freeze new features until the next annual budget
questions.explanation: AWS cost guidance says not every task needs the largest model, and aligning model size to task complexity has cut inference costs by 60 to 80 percent. It also advises avoiding long-term, fixed-quantity contracts in favor of consumption-based pricing while usage is uncertain.
whyWrong: AWS advice is to avoid long fixed-quantity contracts while usage is uncertain.
A same-size model does not match model size to task complexity.
Freezing features gives up value instead of lowering unit cost.

questions.stem: A manufacturer runs Amazon SageMaker AI instances for a quality-inspection model around the clock. Usage has been steady for a year and is expected to stay steady for three more. The finance lead wants a lower rate on this predictable spend. Which option BEST fits?
options: SageMaker AI Savings Plans with a three-year commitment
Seat-based licenses priced per quality inspector each month
Batch processing for the live inspection requests
On-demand rates with no commitment
questions.explanation: SageMaker AI Savings Plans lower prices on SageMaker AI instance usage in return for a one- or three-year commitment to a set amount of usage per hour. Steady, predictable usage is where a commitment pays off.
whyWrong: Seat pricing does not apply to SageMaker instance usage.
Live inspections need immediate results, not batch.
On-demand keeps the highest rate for predictable usage.

questions.stem: Two regional grocers are adopting the same off-the-shelf AI demand-forecasting product. One of them also holds ten years of detailed loyalty-card purchase data that competitors cannot buy. When the strategy team assesses competitive advantage, which factor offers the MOST defensible edge?
options: Early access to the same forecasting product its rival is buying
A bigger marketing budget for the launch
The vendor's brand name in the grocery sector
Loyalty data that rivals cannot easily acquire
questions.explanation: The AWS CAF for AI asks leaders to consider whether their data can provide a defensive moat, something rare and costly for others to get. Proprietary purchase history is that kind of asset, while a product anyone can buy is not.
whyWrong: Rivals can buy the same product, so it is no moat.
Marketing spend does not make the AI hard to copy.
The brand belongs to the vendor and is open to every buyer.

questions.stem: An auto insurer's executive team treats AI as a low priority because its customers have not asked for it. Competitors have started offering instant AI-assisted claim updates. Based on AWS CAF for AI guidance, which factor should the team weigh MOST in its competitive assessment?
options: Customers will likely expect AI features in the near future
Current customer requests are the best guide to future demand
Competitor launches mostly affect their own customers, not ours
Regulatory requirements for insurers should set the pace of AI
questions.explanation: The AWS CAF for AI says customers are likely to raise their expectations of products and services in the near future, and that AI capabilities are part of that expectation. Competitor moves make that shift more likely, not less.
whyWrong: Today's requests do not predict tomorrow's expectations.
Rivals' features shape what customers come to expect.
Waiting on regulation ignores rising customer expectations.

questions.stem: A specialty chemicals firm's CEO wants to wait two years until generative AI settles down before starting any work. Several rivals have already begun small, time-boxed pilots with pretrained models. Which advantage does the firm MOST risk giving up by waiting?
options: Exclusive rights to the foundation models its rivals now use
Lower token prices reserved for early buyers
In-house experience, an AI-ready culture and talent
Exemption from regulatory requirements on AI
questions.explanation: AWS strategy guidance says adopting generative AI early builds experience, expertise, an AI-ready culture and a talent pool, which can give a first-mover advantage. Rivals piloting now are building that head start.
whyWrong: Pretrained models are widely available, so no exclusivity is lost.
The guidance ties early adoption to experience and talent, not to pricing.
Starting early gives no regulatory exemption.

questions.stem: A fitness-equipment maker currently earns its revenue from selling treadmills. Its strategy team proposes using AI on machine usage data to launch a paid, personalized coaching subscription. In the AWS CAF for AI, which transformation domain does this proposal BEST represent?
options: Technology
Process
Organization
Product
questions.explanation: The AWS CAF for AI defines the Product domain as reimagining the business model with new value propositions and revenue models that use AI. A new paid subscription built on AI is a new revenue model.
whyWrong: Technology covers building and enabling AI capability itself.
Process covers improving existing operations, not new offers.
Organization covers how teams coordinate their efforts.

questions.stem: An insurer's AI team now builds new policy-servicing features in days, but every change, from a button label to a pricing rule, passes the same month-long review board. The COO proposes abolishing the board to match the faster pace. What should the transformation lead recommend instead?
options: Remove the review board and let teams release freely
Scale review depth to what a mistake would cost
Buy a faster coding assistant so teams build more changes
Keep the current review process unchanged for safety
questions.explanation: AWS research found that once building gets fast, deciding and approving become the constraint, and that removing a gate and right-sizing it are different answers. The fix is to make oversight proportional to the consequence of being wrong, so low-risk changes move fast while high-risk ones get full review.
whyWrong: Removing a gate is not the same as right-sizing it, and high-risk changes lose review.
Building is no longer the slow part, so faster coding adds to the queue.
A uniform gate turns caution into delay for low-risk changes.

questions.stem: An industrial equipment company's leadership team has funding for one AI proposal this year and wants it to change how the company makes money, not just lower costs. Which proposal is the BEST example of transforming the business model rather than optimizing current operations?
options: Automate invoice matching in the finance team's back office
Sell a maintenance service priced by machine uptime
Summarize internal meeting notes for managers
Speed up drafting of standard sales proposals
questions.explanation: The AWS CAF for AI describes business model transformation as creating new value propositions, products and services, and revenue models that use AI. A paid uptime-based service is a new offer and revenue model, while the others optimize current work.
whyWrong: This makes an existing back-office task cheaper.
This improves internal efficiency, not the offer.
This makes an existing sales task faster.

questions.stem: A food-delivery platform uses AI to recommend dishes. Better recommendations lead to more orders and more loyal customers, and every new order adds data that further improves the recommendations. The strategy team wants a name for this cycle in its board paper. Which concept describes it?
options: AI flywheel
Data silo
Model drift
Pilot fatigue
questions.explanation: The AWS CAF for AI describes the AI flywheel as a virtuous cycle where data trains an AI system, its predictions improve business outcomes, deeper customer relationships follow, and they create more data. That self-reinforcing loop is a source of lasting advantage.
whyWrong: A data silo is data trapped in one team, the opposite of this.
Drift is a decline in model performance over time.
Pilot fatigue is weariness from pilots that never reach production.

questions.stem: A logistics company's strategy director is told that adopting a widely available foundation model will give the company a lasting edge. Every major rival can call the same model at the same prices. Based on the AWS CAF for AI, through which outcomes can AI investment create competitive advantage? (Choose three.)
options: Exclusive access to the foundation model it adopts first
Better insight into what customers need and value
A cost edge from today's model usage rates
Staff who get more done with the same effort
Faster innovation in new products and services
Prestige from partnering with a well-known AI vendor
questions.explanation: The AWS CAF for AI says AI investment can create a competitive advantage through improved customer insight, greater employee efficiency and accelerated innovation. Access to a widely available model, or prices every rival also gets, sets no one apart.
whyWrong: Rivals can call the same model, so access alone sets no one apart.
Rivals pay the same rates, so pricing gives no advantage.
Any rival can partner with the same vendor.

questions.stem: A hospital's billing team plans to add AI to each step of its current 14-step claims process exactly as the process runs today. The CFO wants a lasting operational improvement rather than a one-off gain. What should the billing director recommend?
options: Add AI to every existing step without changing the overall flow
Wait until AI can run the process with no staff
Reimagine the claims process around what AI makes possible
Hire more billing staff to run the current process
questions.explanation: AWS strategy guidance says true value comes from using new technology to reimagine existing processes, not from creating an AI-enabled twin of the current one. Redesigning the flow is what makes the improvement durable.
whyWrong: This builds an AI twin of the old process.
An all-or-nothing wait delays any improvement.
More staff adds cost without changing how work is done.

questions.stem: A regional insurer is starting its first AI program. The CFO wants one precise five-year AI spending figure before approving anything, but usage and prices are hard to predict. Following AWS guidance on how AI costs evolve, what is the BEST approach to setting the investment level?
options: Commit to one fixed five-year figure based on today's prices
Spend nothing until a competitor proves value at full scale
Budget the foundation firmly and plan later spend in ranges
Approve the largest budget possible to outspend competitors
questions.explanation: AWS cost guidance says the first phase is mostly fixed foundation cost that can be budgeted with confidence, and later spend should be planned in conservative, base and aggressive ranges. It also notes that successful companies are neither the biggest nor the smallest spenders.
whyWrong: AI prices and usage shift too fast for a fixed point estimate.
Waiting entirely gives up the learning built in the early phase.
Winners are not the biggest spenders but those tracing spend to value.

questions.stem: Most competitors in a mid-size retail chain's sector already run AI in production, but the chain has made no AI investment yet. Its board is split between one large moonshot project and waiting for the tools to mature further. Following AWS guidance, which investment approach is MOST appropriate?
options: A balanced portfolio of quick wins, strategic bets and a moonshot
A single large moonshot project that receives the whole AI budget at once
No investment until the industry's AI tools fully mature
Copy each competitor's AI purchases one for one
questions.explanation: AWS guidance recommends treating AI as an investment portfolio that balances quick wins, strategic initiatives and moonshots, and warns that in fast-moving fields the cost of inaction often exceeds the risk of calculated experiments. With rivals already in production, a balanced portfolio closes the gap without betting everything on one project.
whyWrong: All-in on one bet concentrates risk with no early wins.
In fast-moving fields the cost of inaction often exceeds the risk.
Copying rivals' tools creates no distinct advantage.

questions.stem: A freight broker's CEO hears that most rivals plan to raise agentic AI spending sharply next year and wants to triple the firm's AI budget at once. The firm has no clear measure of value for its current AI pilots. What should the strategy director advise?
options: Triple the budget now to keep pace with rivals
Cut AI spending until rivals report results
Spend the whole increase on the most expensive models available
Define value measures, then raise spending in stages
questions.explanation: AWS research found that fear of missing out is driving a rush to invest while most organizations lack a clear measure of value, and it advises setting measurable objectives before you begin. Staged increases tied to those measures match investment to competitive pressure without losing control.
whyWrong: Spending driven by fear of missing out lacks any value measure.
Stopping entirely cedes ground in a market that is moving.
Model price is not a measure of business value.

questions.stem: A property listing platform uses generative AI to draft home descriptions from agents' notes and photos. The marketing director finds that some drafts mention a pool, a garage or a sea view that the home does not have. Buyers have started to complain. Which responsible AI dimension does this problem MOST directly put at risk?
