options: Fairness across the buyer groups who read the listings
Veracity and robustness of the generated content
Transparency about the use of AI in the listings
Controllability of how agents steer the draft generator
questions.explanation: AWS defines veracity and robustness as achieving correct system outputs, even with unexpected inputs. Descriptions that invent features are incorrect outputs, so this is the dimension at risk.
whyWrong: Nothing suggests one group of buyers is treated differently from another.
Disclosing AI use would not stop the drafts from stating false features.
The issue is wrong content in the output, not a lack of ways to steer the system.

questions.stem: A regional bank uses a model to set credit limits on new card applications. Customer-service staff report that declined applicants keep asking why, and loan officers can only say the model scored them low. The product owner wants to fix this gap before expanding the program. Which responsible AI dimension should she prioritize?
options: Transparency that a model was used in the decision
Privacy and security of the applicant data it reads
Safety of the model against misuse by staff
Explainability of the factors behind each score
questions.explanation: AWS describes explainability as understanding and evaluating system outputs. Officers who cannot say which factors drove a score have an explainability gap, which is what applicants are running into.
whyWrong: Applicants already know a model was used and lack only the reason for the result.
The complaint is about understanding outcomes, not about how data is protected.
Nothing in the scenario points to harmful output or misuse.

questions.stem: An HR director pilots an AI assistant that summarizes job applicants' CVs for hiring managers. A review finds two problems: applicants from some postcodes are rated lower for similar experience, and summaries repeat applicants' home addresses and health notes. Which TWO responsible AI dimensions do these findings raise? (Choose two.)
options: Fairness toward different applicant groups
Transparency to applicants that AI is used
Veracity of the experience each summary reports
Safety against harmful language in rejection letters
Privacy of the personal details in each CV
questions.explanation: Rating similar applicants differently by postcode is a fairness issue, which AWS defines as considering impacts on different groups of stakeholders. Repeating addresses and health notes is a privacy issue, about appropriately obtaining, using and protecting data.
whyWrong: Nothing says applicants were misled about AI use.
The review found no misstatement of applicants' experience.
No harmful or toxic output is described in the review.

questions.stem: A card issuer's fraud system can block suspicious payments within seconds, but faster blocking also stops more genuine purchases. The fraud lead and the customer-experience lead argue case by case about which matters more, and every release is delayed. What should the program director do to resolve this MOST effectively?
options: Agree written criteria on which goal wins in which situations
Let the data scientists choose whichever threshold scores best
Maximize blocking speed now and review complaints next quarter
Pause the project until both goals can be fully met
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says to develop explicit trade-off criteria, like tenets, that reflect organizational policies and stakeholder needs. Its own example is fraud detection weighing a higher false positive rate against a faster response, and agreed criteria stop the case-by-case argument.
whyWrong: This hands a business trade-off to a technical team with no agreed criteria.
This picks a side by default and leaves the harm to genuine customers unmanaged.
Competing goals rarely both reach their maximum, so this stalls the program.

questions.stem: A hospital group's AI imaging tool is highly accurate on three common lung conditions but unreliable on rare ones. The chief medical officer wants it to cover every condition at launch so no patient group is left out, while clinicians worry about missed rare cases. What is the MOST appropriate way forward?
options: Launch for every condition and add a general accuracy disclaimer
Delay launch until rare-condition accuracy matches the common ones
Launch for the three reliable conditions and state its limits
Ask engineers to lower thresholds so rare cases get flagged
questions.explanation: AWS recommends narrowing to the minimum viable use case that still delivers meaningful value while reducing risk, such as one specific condition type. Launching where the tool is reliable, with documented limits, keeps the value and avoids unreliable rare-case results.
whyWrong: A disclaimer does not stop unreliable results on rare conditions from reaching clinicians.
This gives up proven value while waiting for a goal that may never be reached.
This is a technical tweak that does not settle the scope decision.

questions.stem: A retailer's marketing VP wants to approve AI-driven offers that combine purchase history, browsing data and phone location. The privacy officer objects that customers never expected location to be used this way. The VP proposes approving now and settling privacy later. What should the steering group do FIRST?
options: Approve the full data set now and review privacy after launch
Weigh benefits and risks for each stakeholder group
Let the offer vendor decide which data its model needs
Drop location and personalize from purchases and browsing
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says to review objectives, benefits and risks across responsible AI dimensions and stakeholders to find conflicts, then weigh the trade-off. That step comes before any approval, so the group can decide with the privacy cost in view.
whyWrong: This bolts privacy on after customers are already affected.
The vendor does not own the company's trade-off between value and privacy.
This settles the trade-off before benefits and risks are weighed.

questions.stem: A logistics firm is building an AI route planner that also scores driver behavior. The project plan schedules the responsible AI review for the week before launch, after design and testing are finished. The program manager asks when the review should happen. What is the BEST answer?
options: Keep it before launch and add a yearly post-launch audit
Hold it after the first driver complaints arrive
Replace it with a certificate from the AI vendor
Start it at design and continue it through operations
questions.explanation: The AWS Responsible AI Lens embeds responsible AI practices throughout the lifecycle, from design through operations. It puts special emphasis on identifying and resolving potential issues in design, not just before launch.
whyWrong: Issues found that late are costly to fix, and the design stage is skipped.
This waits for harm before acting.
The firm cannot hand its own responsible AI duties to a vendor.

questions.stem: A CFO reviewing an AI program objects that responsible AI work is adding cost months before any system reaches production. She asks the AI lead why the company should not defer it until a system proves its value. According to the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework for AI, which response is MOST accurate?
options: The work can wait until the system is proven in production
Responsible AI applies only to systems that face customers
The early cost pays off in the mid-term by limiting damage
The vendor's responsible AI work covers the company's duties
questions.explanation: The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework for AI says to address responsible AI early in the AI journey and throughout its lifecycle. It notes that this cost builds up before production but pays off in the mid-term by mitigating damage.
whyWrong: AWS says to address responsible AI early and throughout the lifecycle, not after.
AWS frames it as part of the whole AI journey, not one class of system.
AWS says to ask how the vendor handled it, not to rely on it in place of your own work.

questions.stem: An insurer's digital team ships small AI prototypes to test users every two weeks. The governance lead proposes adopting the 'responsible by design' principle from the AWS Well-Architected Responsible AI Lens. The team objects that it will end their fast release cycle. Which response from the governance lead is MOST accurate?
options: It requires a full risk sign-off before each prototype is built
It moves responsible AI checks to the final release gate
It allows fast prototyping with open, transparent iteration
It lets prototypes skip review until they reach customers
questions.explanation: The Lens says responsible by design embeds responsible AI practices from design through operations, with emphasis on resolving issues in design. It states that this does not preclude rapid prototype-and-release development, but it does encourage open, transparent iteration.
whyWrong: The Lens says the principle does not preclude rapid prototype-and-release processes.
The principle stresses finding and fixing issues at design, not at the end.
The Lens embeds responsible AI practices from design onward, early builds included.

questions.stem: An insurer uses AI to recommend payouts on property claims. Most claims are small and routine, but some are large, unusual or scored with low confidence. The claims director has a fixed number of adjusters and must decide where human review adds the most value. What is the BEST approach?
options: Route large, unusual or low-confidence claims to adjusters
Have adjusters approve every claim before any payment is made
Review a small random sample of claims once each quarter
Remove adjusters from the process once accuracy passes 95 percent
questions.explanation: AWS guidance places human review where outputs are harder to judge or where errors have significant consequences. It also says reviewers should get explanations and confidence scores so they can decide well.
whyWrong: Reviewing everything spreads scarce adjusters across routine cases.
This misses the high-stakes cases that most need a person.
High overall accuracy does not make the costly, hard cases safe.

questions.stem: A bank's AI operations head is writing the protocol for when automated monitoring alerts on a lending model must go to a human reviewer. She wants triggers that are set in advance rather than left to whoever is on shift. Which THREE factors should the triggers be based on? (Choose three.)
options: Size of the review team on shift
Severity of the alert
Model confidence below a set threshold
How long the model has been in production
Business impact of the affected decision
Order in which alerts reached the queue
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says to configure human review triggers based on alert severity, confidence thresholds and business impact. It pairs these with escalation paths that set clear decision authority.
whyWrong: Staffing levels do not change how much a given alert matters.
Model age does not change how much a given alert matters.
Arrival order is not a measure of risk.

questions.stem: A pharmacy chain plans a public chatbot that answers questions about over-the-counter medicines using its approved product leaflets. In testing, it sometimes states dosage details that appear in no leaflet. The digital director needs a safeguard before launch. Which safeguard is MOST appropriate?
options: Add a notice asking customers to check answers with a pharmacist
Limit the chatbot to the twenty most-asked questions
Switch to a larger model that knows more about drugs
Check each answer against the source before it is shown
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers contextual grounding checks that detect and filter hallucinations based on grounding in a source. Checking answers against the approved leaflets stops invented dosage details before they reach customers.
whyWrong: A notice leaves invented dosage advice in front of customers.
Invented dosage details can still appear in those answers.
A bigger model can still invent details that are not in the leaflets.

questions.stem: A manufacturer's CIO proposes an AI governance board made up only of IT architects and data scientists. The board would oversee responsible AI and alignment with AI regulation across the company. The chief operating officer is asked to approve the charter. What change should she request?
options: Keep it technical and brief the business leaders each quarter
Hand oversight to the AI vendor's own ethics team
Add legal, HR, procurement and regulatory affairs members
Add more data scientists to cover more of the models
questions.explanation: The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework for AI recommends an AI governance board with representation from multiple business units. Its examples include research, human resources, legal, government and regulatory affairs, procurement and communications.
whyWrong: One-way briefings leave legal, people and regulatory views out of decisions.
The vendor cannot be accountable for the company's use of AI.
More technical members do not add the missing business perspectives.

questions.stem: A healthcare company is creating a model governance committee to oversee which foundation models its teams may use. The chief data officer is drafting the committee's charter and wants it to match AWS guidance for enterprise generative AI adoption. Which THREE responsibilities belong in the charter? (Choose three.)
options: Set evaluation criteria for foundation models
Write the prompts for each business application
Approve the annual IT budget for every department
Review teams' requests to use models
Configure network settings for each model endpoint
Validate compliance with ethical AI principles
questions.explanation: AWS describes a model governance committee that develops evaluation criteria for foundation models, reviews usage requests and validates compliance with ethical AI principles. It works closely with legal and compliance teams on performance and risk.
whyWrong: Prompt writing is delivery work for product teams, not a governance duty.
Departmental budgets sit with finance and leadership, not a model committee.
Network configuration is an engineering task outside the committee's role.

questions.stem: Three business units at a retailer run their own generative AI assistants. When one assistant gave customers wrong return terms, nobody could say who was answerable, and each unit pointed to the others. The CEO asks what to put in place first to prevent a repeat. What is the BEST answer?
options: A new monitoring tool installed on the three assistants
Executive accountability and a cross-functional review board
A rule that each business unit self-certifies its own assistant
A pause on all assistants until AI law is settled
questions.explanation: AWS describes a three-layer approach in which governance and culture set the foundation. That layer starts with clear executive accountability and cross-functional review boards, before process and tooling.
whyWrong: Tools help later, but they do not settle who is answerable.
Self-certification keeps governance fragmented across units.
This halts value without fixing the accountability gap.

questions.stem: A software firm plans to add AI candidate screening to its hiring product. Clients are in three EU countries and two US states, and applicant data is processed in a fourth country. The product lead's proposal lists the regulatory scope simply as 'global'. What should the firm do FIRST?
options: Name each country and state, then confirm rules with legal
Launch in the US first and check EU rules after launch
Rely on the cloud provider's existing compliance certifications
Apply one internal rule set across the markets it serves
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says to identify where data is collected and processed and where decisions apply, naming specific countries and states rather than a global scope. The team should then work with legal to find the requirements in each location.
whyWrong: This delays the legal check until after the system is already in use.
The provider's certifications do not cover the firm's own use case.
A single internal rule set ignores the laws that apply in each place.

questions.stem: A hospital network operating in the EU uses AI for two things: a chatbot that tells staff the cafeteria menu, and a tool that helps clinicians interpret test results. The compliance director is briefing the board on how the EU AI Act treats these uses. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: Both face the same duties as AI systems used in a hospital setting
Neither is covered unless the model was trained in the EU
The menu chatbot faces the stricter rules as it is used more often
The clinical tool faces a higher bar, such as human oversight
questions.explanation: AWS describes the EU AI Act as risk-based, with high-risk applications such as healthcare given a higher regulatory bar. That bar can include human-in-the-loop requirements, while a low-stakes chatbot is not held to the same standard.
whyWrong: The Act is risk-based, so duties differ with the use, not the setting.
Where a model was trained does not decide whether a use is covered.
The Act scales duties to risk, not to how often a tool is used.

questions.stem: A fintech's home market has no AI-specific law yet, but regulators have signaled that rules are coming. The head of compliance wants to prepare without guessing at the final text and asks the AI steering group for a direction. Which direction is MOST appropriate according to AWS guidance?
options: Hold off on any AI controls until the local law is final
Copy a competitor's published AI policy without changes
Align its AI risk practices with the NIST AI RMF now
Rely on its existing data protection policy for AI risk
questions.explanation: AWS advises aligning your risk framework with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework while adapting controls for AI-specific challenges. Its guidance on regulatory change also encourages using NIST ahead of regulatory actions.
whyWrong: Waiting leaves AI risk unmanaged and leaves the firm behind when rules arrive.
Another firm's policy is not built around this firm's risks.
AWS says controls must be adapted for AI-specific risks.

questions.stem: A marketing team uses a free public image generator to create rough mock-ups for campaigns. Leadership has approved the tool for this purpose, but the company has no enterprise agreement with its provider. The marketing director asks what data rule staff should follow. Using the AWS AI Security Scoping Matrix, what is the MOST appropriate rule?
options: Upload unreleased product photos if the paid tier is used
Use only public, non-proprietary data in the tool
Upload customer photos once their names are removed
Pause use until an enterprise contract is signed
questions.explanation: The Scoping Matrix places public consumer apps, free or paid, in Scope 1, where you do not own or see the model or its training data. For Scope 1 it advises prioritizing public, non-proprietary data, as providers may use submitted data to improve their models or services.
whyWrong: Scope 1 covers paid consumer services too, and the photos stay proprietary.
Customer images are still proprietary data a provider may use.
The approved use can continue safely with public data.

questions.stem: A bank's risk committee is reviewing a proposal to build a customer-service assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Members worry that prompts containing account details will be used to train the model provider's models. The CIO must answer accurately before the vote. Which statement is correct?
options: Bedrock shares the bank's prompts with model providers for quality review
The commitment covers fine-tuned models but not prompts
AWS handles access control for the bank's Bedrock users
Prompts don't train base models or go to any model provider
questions.explanation: AWS states that with Amazon Bedrock, customer content is not used to improve the base models and is not shared with any model providers. Data is also encrypted in transit and at rest.
whyWrong: AWS states content is not shared with any model providers.
The commitment covers Bedrock content, prompts included.
Under shared responsibility, the bank still controls access to its content.

questions.stem: An insurer is moving its internal claims assistant to Amazon Bedrock. The governance lead is drafting a policy that separates what AWS handles from what the insurer must still own under the shared responsibility model. Which TWO items stay with the insurer? (Choose two.)
options: Protecting the physical data centers that run the service
Giving each user only the access their job needs
Logging user and API activity for audit
Securing model providers' software in Bedrock's deployment accounts
Maintaining the global network that AWS operates
questions.explanation: AWS says the shared responsibility model applies to Bedrock: AWS protects the infrastructure, and the customer keeps control of its content and security configuration. AWS recommends giving each user only the permissions needed for their job and logging API and user activity with AWS CloudTrail.
whyWrong: AWS is responsible for the global infrastructure that runs the cloud.
Those accounts are owned and operated by the Bedrock service team.
The network is part of the infrastructure AWS protects.

questions.stem: An insurer's governance lead has listed twelve potential harms for a generative AI claims assistant, from rude replies to wrongful claim denials. The mitigation budget will not cover all twelve this year. She must explain to the steering group how to decide what comes first. What is the BEST approach?
options: Address the harms in the same order the teams reported them
Spread the mitigation budget evenly across all twelve harms
Rate harms by likelihood and severity, then fix the worst
Start with whichever harms the engineers can fix the fastest
questions.explanation: AWS guidance rates each harm on likelihood and severity in a risk matrix to give a level such as low, medium, high or critical. Mitigation is then prioritized by those ratings, highest risks first, while also weighing cost and feasibility.
whyWrong: Reporting order has nothing to do with how risky each harm is.
Equal funding under-protects the harms that matter most.
Ease of fixing can inform the plan, but risk level should lead it.

questions.stem: A utility company is starting its fourth generative AI use case. Each earlier team assessed risks from scratch in its own format, and similar harms received very different ratings. The chief risk officer wants future assessments to be faster and more consistent. What should she put in place?
options: A shared risk registry checked at each new use case
Separate risk notes kept by each team in its own chosen format
A default high-risk rating for each new use case
An outside assessment of the largest project only
questions.explanation: AWS recommends a risk registry that records each risk with its use case, harmful examples, stakeholders, likelihood, severity, level and mitigation. Consulting it when starting a new use case speeds up and calibrates the assessment.
whyWrong: This keeps the inconsistency she wants to remove.
Uniform ratings ignore real differences and waste effort on low-risk cases.
One external review does not give teams a common record to build on.

questions.stem: A travel company plans to use one foundation model in two places: an internal search tool for its own agents, and a public chatbot for travelers on its website. The governance lead asks whether both should get the same controls, as they share a model. What is the BEST answer?
options: Use identical controls for both as the model is the same
Set controls by exposure, stricter for the public chatbot
Put the stricter controls on the internal tool, which sees company data
Wait for incidents to show which one needs more control
questions.explanation: AWS advises calibrating risk strategy to deployment context and user exposure, noting internal applications warrant different controls than public-facing ones. It adds that safety controls may need stricter thresholds than traditional security measures.
whyWrong: The model is shared, but the deployment context and exposure differ.
The public chatbot reaches outside users and warrants the stricter controls.
This waits for harm instead of planning controls by risk.

questions.stem: A utility's generative AI billing assistant is in production, and its monitoring captures hallucination rates, PII flags and latency. Alerts go to a forty-person mailing list. When a PII alert fired last month, each recipient assumed someone else was handling it, and nobody acted for a week. What should the head of operations put in place?
options: Track more risk metrics in the monitoring system
Send the alerts to the AI vendor's support desk
Give each alert a named owner and a runbook
Review the month's alerts at a monthly operations meeting
questions.explanation: AWS describes production monitoring as capture, alerts and response, with alerts directed to the relevant stakeholders with an actionable outcome. It recommends runbooks attached to each alert to help teams find the root cause and respond.
whyWrong: More signals do not help when no one owns the response.
The vendor does not own the company's response to its own data risks.
A monthly review is too slow for alerts that need action now.

questions.stem: A COO is reviewing the monitoring dashboard for a generative AI claims assistant now in production. It shows uptime, latency and error rates, and she asks what else it must track to cover risk and value properly. Which TWO additions BEST match AWS monitoring guidance? (Choose two.)
options: Adoption, satisfaction and measurable business impact
Number of prompts engineers wrote during development
Lines of code changed in each release of the app
PII use, consent and policy violations
Model vendor's published benchmark scores each quarter
questions.explanation: AWS describes pillars beyond system health, including business and user-interaction health and compliance and risk indicators. These track adoption and business impact, and PII use, consent and policy violations.
whyWrong: Development activity says nothing about how the live system performs.
Code churn is not an AWS monitoring pillar for business or risk health.
Vendor benchmarks do not show how this system performs for this business.

questions.stem: A newly hired CISO at a bank discovers that several business units use AI tools, and some were never approved. She has been asked to put risk controls on AI quickly. Before choosing any controls, what should she do FIRST?
options: Issue a policy banning unapproved tools and enforce it
Buy a monitoring platform that covers only the approved tools
Inventory all AI in use, approved and unapproved
Ask each unit to name the one tool it uses most
questions.explanation: AWS security guidance says to start by knowing where AI is running, auditing all AI workloads, approved and shadow. It recommends keeping a model inventory as the base for controls.
whyWrong: A ban without knowing what exists is hard to enforce and drives use underground.
This leaves the unapproved tools, often the riskiest, unseen.
One tool per unit misses most of what is running.

questions.stem: A lender's credit model passed a bias review before launch last year. The data science manager now proposes dropping further bias checks to save effort, arguing the model has not changed. The head of model risk disagrees. Which TWO points support her position? (Choose two.)
options: The model's unchanged code keeps its bias results stable
A launch-time bias check alone may not be sufficient
Bias checks can wait until the model is next retrained
A rise in complaints is an adequate early bias signal
Bias metrics need regular checks with alert thresholds
questions.explanation: AWS notes that bias can be introduced in deployed models when live data differs from training data, so measuring bias only at train-and-deploy time might not be sufficient. It recommends monitoring bias metrics at regular intervals with alerts when they cross a threshold.
whyWrong: Bias can grow as live data shifts, even with no change to the model.
Live data can drift long before a planned retrain.
Monitoring with alerts can find bias before complaints arrive.

questions.stem: A staffing firm's candidate-ranking model passed a balanced bias audit at launch. Since then it has been retrained each month on which candidates recruiters click. Over a year, its top results have shifted toward one profile, and other qualified applicants rank lower. The operations director asks where the bias most likely came from. What is the MOST likely source?
options: The original applicant data the model was first trained on
A feedback loop from retraining on recruiter clicks
Growth in the number of applicants applying each month
The cloud region where the model is hosted
questions.explanation: The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework for AI lists hidden feedback loops among the risks inherent to AI, alongside unexpected outcomes that affect groups of people negatively. Here, monthly retraining on recruiters' clicks lets earlier rankings shape later ones, while the launch audit rules out the original data.
whyWrong: The launch audit found that data balanced, and the skew grew later.
Volume alone does not tilt rankings toward one profile.
Hosting location has no effect on how candidates are ranked.

questions.stem: After a merger, an insurer will use its claims-triage model on a newly acquired customer segment. The risk lead is writing the bias-check plan and wants a checkpoint at each stage where AWS says bias can be detected. Which THREE checkpoints should the plan include? (Choose three.)
options: When a regulator requests a bias review
During data preparation, before training
After customer complaints about claim outcomes
After training, before the model is deployed
When the merger's integration project closes
In production, on the model's live decisions
questions.explanation: AWS says SageMaker Clarify can detect potential bias during data preparation, after model training and in the deployed model. Checking all three matters here, as live data from the new segment may differ from what the model learned.
whyWrong: Waiting for a regulator leaves bias unchecked in the meantime.
Complaints arrive after customers have already been affected.
Project milestones are not tied to when bias can appear.

questions.stem: A publisher's marketing team uses an AWS generative AI service listed as covered by AWS's IP indemnity. To get faster drafts, the team wants to switch off the service's available filters. The general counsel is asked whether this matters for IP protection. What is the MOST accurate answer?
options: Filter settings change output quality but not the IP cover
Disabling available filters can void the indemnity
IP cover depends on the model chosen, not its settings
The indemnity covers the inputs the team supplies
questions.explanation: AWS defends customers against third-party IP claims over output from listed generative AI services. The terms say this does not apply if the customer interferes with or fails to enable available filters.
whyWrong: Failing to enable available filters is a named exclusion from the indemnity.
Coverage also depends on not disabling the available filters.
It covers output, and claims from infringing inputs are excluded.

questions.stem: A media company is choosing a generative AI writing tool for its editors. Legal wants two IP-related questions added to the vendor review, and the procurement lead asks which matter most before the shortlist is signed off. Which TWO questions should be added? (Choose two.)
options: How it keeps our unpublished drafts from leaking
How quickly it drafts a full-length article
Whether it connects to our publishing system
How it limits output copying others' copyright
How its price per seat compares with rival writing tools
questions.explanation: The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework for AI lists copyright infringement and model data leakage among the concerns to watch for when using a foundation model. It also says to ask how the vendor took a responsible AI approach.
whyWrong: Speed is a fair procurement question but not an IP risk.
Integration is a fair procurement question but not an IP risk.
Price is a fair procurement question but not an IP risk.

questions.stem: An education company is launching a public homework-help chatbot for children. Parents' groups worry it could produce or respond to violent or hateful content. The product director must pick a safeguard before the fixed launch date. Which safeguard is MOST appropriate?
options: Filter the children's prompts and trust the model's own replies
Rely on users reporting harmful replies after they appear
Apply content filters and denied topics to prompts and replies
Train a new model from scratch on curated school texts
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails content filters help block harmful text such as hate and violence, and denied topics block undesirable subjects. These safeguards can protect both user inputs and model responses.
whyWrong: Harmful content can come from the model's replies as well as prompts.
This acts only after children have seen the content.
Building a new model is costly and still needs output safeguards.

questions.stem: An HR team's generative AI assistant uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the company's HR document library. Employees report that it sometimes quotes leave rules from a handbook that was replaced last year. Both the old and the new handbooks still sit in the library. What should the HR director do FIRST?
options: Switch to a larger model that reasons more carefully
Remove old versions and keep the library current
Ask staff to confirm each leave answer with the HR team
Fine-tune the model on the new handbook's contents
questions.explanation: AWS describes RAG as retrieving from authoritative knowledge sources and warns that this external data can become stale. It advises updating the documents through automated or periodic processes to keep retrieved information current. Removing the replaced handbook stops the assistant drawing on outdated rules.
whyWrong: A bigger model still retrieves whichever handbook the library holds.
This shifts work back to HR and leaves wrong answers in place.
The old handbook would still be retrieved, and fine-tuning is costly to repeat.

questions.stem: A telecom's support center uses a model to route tickets to the right team. Each time new products launch, monitoring flags drift and misrouting rises. Each time, the team then spends weeks debating whether to retrain while customers wait. The operations director wants a lasting way to respond once drift is detected. What should she put in place?
options: Set drift thresholds that trigger retraining or rollback
Retrain the model on a fixed yearly schedule
Raise the alert threshold until drift is flagged less often
Replace the model with fixed rules for each product
questions.explanation: The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework for AI notes that model drift often happens over time and suggests defining thresholds for retraining. When performance drifts beyond the acceptable threshold, automated validation can trigger retraining or rollback to a previous version.
whyWrong: A fixed date ignores when drift actually crosses an acceptable level.
This hides the drift instead of responding to it.
Rules would need rewriting at each launch and give up the model's value.

questions.stem: A bank plans a customer chatbot that answers questions about account fees. In testing, it sometimes quotes fees that do not exist. The digital banking lead must cut this risk before launch without giving up the service. Which THREE measures should she prioritize? (Choose three.)
options: Fine-tune the model on a year of past customer chats
Switch to the largest model the vendor offers
Ground replies in the bank's current fee documents
Add a notice that quoted fees may vary by account
Write clear, specific prompts with context
Apply guardrails that evaluate responses
questions.explanation: AWS lists retrieval-augmented generation and clear, specific prompts with context as ways to prevent hallucinations. It adds that Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock evaluates model responses against use-case policies as an extra layer of safeguards.
whyWrong: Past chats may contain the same wrong fees.
A bigger model still lacks the bank's fee schedule.
A notice leaves wrong fees in front of customers.

questions.stem: A logistics company's COO wants to roll out AI agents across dispatch next quarter. Leaders are enthusiastic and budget is approved. A readiness assessment finds dispatch data spread across regional systems that don't connect, and no agreed structure for governing agent decisions. What should the COO do FIRST?
options: Fix the flagged foundations before setting a rollout date
Launch on schedule and fix data and governance issues as they come up
Buy a more capable model to make up for weak data
Start agents in one region now and add governance once results come in
questions.explanation: AWS research found that leaders are keen on AI while few rate their data architecture or governance structures as ready. Its advice is to invest in foundations such as data architecture and governance structures. Here those gaps, not enthusiasm or model choice, are what will block the rollout.
whyWrong: Fixing foundations after launch puts an ungoverned agent into live dispatch work.
A stronger model does not fix disconnected data or missing governance.
Governance added after launch is bolted on, and the data gaps remain.

questions.stem: A regional retailer's CFO will not fund an AI program until the strategy lead shows the company is ready to adopt it. The strategy lead is planning a readiness assessment and wants it to cover the dimensions that most often decide whether AI adoption succeeds. Which areas should the assessment examine? (Choose three.)
options: Whether leaders agree on what AI should achieve
Whether IT has already picked a preferred foundation model
Whether the data AI would use is accurate and complete
Whether a shortlist of AI vendors is ready for review
Whether staff are open to new ways of working
Whether a launch date for the first AI tool is set
questions.explanation: The exam guide names leadership alignment, data quality, cultural preparedness, technical infrastructure and governance frameworks as critical readiness dimensions. A chosen model, a vendor shortlist or a launch date are plans and purchases, not evidence that the company can adopt AI.
whyWrong: Choosing a model is a technology decision, not a sign the company is ready.
A vendor shortlist shows what is for sale, not whether the company can adopt AI.
A launch date is a plan, not evidence of readiness.

questions.stem: An insurer runs three generative AI applications in production. Each has alerts when it misbehaves, a team on call to fix problems, staff who review risky outputs and a signed-off responsible AI policy. However, each new project starts from scratch, and other departments have not adopted AI. Which level best describes the insurer's AI deployment?
options: Envision
Experiment
Launch
Scale
questions.explanation: Launch means a few applications in production with governance, monitoring, support teams and a human-in-the-loop process. Scale adds broad adoption across departments, reusable components and self-service, which the insurer still lacks.
whyWrong: Envision has no formal projects, but the insurer runs apps in production.
Experiment is about pilots and proofs of concept, not governed production apps.
Scale needs many departments and reusable, self-service components, which are missing.

questions.stem: A manufacturer's board asks the transformation director for a single AI maturity grade. The platform team already offers reusable AI components through self-service, but governance consists only of preliminary guidelines, and most staff have had no AI training. How should the director report the company's maturity?
options: Average the aspects into one overall maturity level
Report where each aspect sits on its own
Report the highest level any aspect has reached
Report the lowest level as the company's single grade
questions.explanation: The AWS maturity model says each aspect of adoption should be considered independently, and one organization can show characteristics of different levels. A single grade would hide that governance and people lag far behind the platform.
whyWrong: An average hides the gaps the board most needs to see.
The strongest aspect overstates readiness in governance and skills.
One low grade understates the platform and still hides where the gaps lie.

questions.stem: A manufacturer's AI team built a defect-report summary tool in two weeks. It then waited four months for plant-level sign-offs, an architecture board and change approval before anyone on the floor could use it. The company already has a published responsible AI policy. Executives now propose hiring more data scientists to speed up delivery. Which capability gap is MOST holding the manufacturer back?
options: A people gap in data science skills
A technology gap in model capability
A process gap in review and approval
A governance gap from missing AI policy
questions.explanation: Building was fast and the delay came from review and approval steps. AWS research found that once building gets fast, the cost of deciding, governing and approving the work becomes the bottleneck. More data scientists would only build faster into the same queue.
whyWrong: The tool was built in two weeks, so skills were not the constraint.
The tool worked; the delay came after it was built.
The manufacturer already has a published responsible AI policy.

questions.stem: Before rolling out AI tools, the COO of a mid-sized insurer asks each division to map signs of organizational debt that would slow adoption. The divisions return a long list of findings, and the COO wants to deal with the true organizational debt items first. Which findings are signs of organizational debt? (Choose two.)
options: Customer records sit in two databases that do not connect
Teams resist change and cling to old ways of working
The company's preferred foundation model is nearing its end-of-life date
Cloud capacity for model hosting is limited in one region
Routine decisions need several layers of sign-off over weeks
questions.explanation: AWS describes organizational debt as outdated processes, rigid hierarchies and cultural resistance to change, including too many approval layers. Adding AI on top of these compounds the debt rather than transforming the business.
whyWrong: Disconnected databases are a data silo, a data readiness issue.
Model end-of-life is a technology continuity issue.
Hosting capacity is an infrastructure issue, not organizational debt.

questions.stem: A healthcare network has finished its first year of AI awareness work. Leaders attended training, AI champions are named, and a long list of possible use cases exists, but there are no formal projects yet. The CIO now has budget to move the network to the next maturity level. Which investment fits BEST?
options: Build a self-service AI platform that each department can use at once
Hire a research team to train the network's own foundation model
Buy enterprise AI licenses for the whole workforce at once
Fund a cross-functional squad to test top use cases in small pilots
questions.explanation: The network is at Envision. AWS's path to the next level is to form cross-functional squads, shortlist the top use cases, fund small proofs of concept and define success metrics for each. A platform for everyone or a custom model skips the step of proving value.
whyWrong: A self-service platform belongs at Scale, before any use case is proven.
Training its own model is a technology-first leap at this stage.
Licensing everyone at once is all-or-nothing, with no proven use case yet.

questions.stem: A retailer's transformation lead has a one-year roadmap with fourteen AI initiatives running in parallel: a new platform, a center of excellence, a data mesh and eleven use cases. Halfway through, staff are overwhelmed and morale is dropping. According to the AWS CAF for AI, what should the lead do?
options: Keep the vision but sequence smaller steps with measurable KPIs
Keep all fourteen initiatives and add contractors to cover the load
Pause the initiatives until the data mesh is complete
Drop the long-term vision and focus on near-term cost savings
questions.explanation: CAF-AI warns that trying to do everything in the same cycle can lead to discouragement in the organization. It recommends pairing a larger picture with many pragmatic steps that each have measurable KPIs, evolving capabilities as you progress.
whyWrong: More people do not fix trying to do everything at once.
Halting everything on one dependency stalls all progress and value.
CAF-AI says to stay ambitious, so dropping the vision overcorrects.

questions.stem: A hospital's facilities director wants an AI model to predict rare failures of imaging equipment. Only a handful of failures have ever been logged, and past technicians recorded them inconsistently. A vendor says its platform can start training next month. According to AWS responsible AI guidance, what should the director do?
options: Start training next month and let the model learn from live equipment data
Reframe the use case or weigh non-AI alternatives
Choose the largest available model to make up for the thin data
Buy another hospital's failure model and apply it unchanged
questions.explanation: The Responsible AI Lens says that if reliable training and test examples are hard to get, you may not have the data to develop or evaluate an AI system. It advises reframing the use case or considering alternate solutions. Data readiness is the gap, not the platform.
whyWrong: Without reliable examples there is no sound way to train or test the model.
A bigger model does not create reliable examples that do not exist.
A model built on another hospital's data has not been evaluated on this equipment.

questions.stem: A fast-growing distributor wants AI forecasting, but each division keeps its own spreadsheets and systems. Reports conflict, staff copy data by hand, and divisions skipped data rules during rapid growth. The chief data officer is choosing from actions AWS describes for breaking down data silos. Which actions should the chief data officer take? (Choose two.)
options: Restrict data access to a small central IT team
Promote a data-sharing culture led from the top down
Suspend data rules again to speed up the forecasting pilot
Let each division keep choosing its own storage tools and formats
Set up data governance with clear roles and rules for sharing
questions.explanation: AWS lists a data governance structure that defines roles and rules, and a data-sharing culture led from the top down, among the ways to break down silos. Ignoring data rules during rapid scaling is one of the causes it names.
whyWrong: Locking data to one small team keeps others from reaching it.
Skipping data rules under pressure is a named cause of silos.
Separate tool choices are what created the silos.

questions.stem: A retailer's AI pilot for product descriptions has stalled. No one can say who may approve using supplier catalog data, and the merchandising and e-commerce teams define an 'active product' differently. The program lead wants to fix the root cause rather than work around it pilot by pilot. Which step addresses it BEST?
options: Ask data engineers to choose a new data integration tool
Let each pilot team define the terms it needs locally
Name a data owner to set access rules and key terms
Have the AI vendor decide which data the model may use
questions.explanation: AWS describes data owners as the people who make policies about data, including who should have access and under what circumstances, and key term definitions. Both blockers in the pilot are decisions a data owner makes.
whyWrong: A tool does not settle who approves access or what terms mean.
Local definitions create more conflict between teams.
Data access decisions belong to the company, not a vendor.

questions.stem: A bank's central data team is overwhelmed by requests from business lines that want data for AI. The chief data officer proposes moving to a data mesh. Before the executive committee votes, members ask what the model actually involves. Which statements describe a data mesh? (Choose three.)
options: Each domain sets its own standards with no shared rules
Federated governance sets standards across domains
Domains keep their data to themselves and do not share it
Each business domain owns and serves its own data
A central team ingests and transforms data on behalf of each domain
Domains share data as products under common standards
questions.explanation: AWS defines a data mesh by domain ownership, data productization, self-service and federated governance. Each domain serves its own data to others while conforming to organization-wide standards, instead of a central team ingesting everything.
whyWrong: A mesh still conforms to organization-wide standards.
A mesh exists to share data across domains, not lock it in.
Central ingestion is the model a data mesh moves away from.

questions.stem: A marketing director wants generative AI to draft campaign copy using existing foundation models. The team has no plans to train its own model and no staff to run machine learning infrastructure. IT asks the director to state the platform requirement at a business level. Which approach fits BEST?
options: Pick one platform now for every future AI workload company-wide
Host open-weight models on self-managed servers to keep full control
Train a custom model in Amazon SageMaker AI before any pilot
Use a managed service like Amazon Bedrock with nothing to operate
questions.explanation: AWS's decision guide says Amazon Bedrock is the default starting point for inference on available models, with no infrastructure to operate. It advises choosing the most managed option that gives the control you need, and making the choice per workload rather than once for the organization.
whyWrong: AWS advises choosing per workload, not once for the whole company.
Self-managed hosting adds full operational responsibility the team cannot carry.
Training a model is not needed when existing models do the job.

questions.stem: A utility's AI pilots are run by IT with support from several mid-level managers. Two pilots have stalled because business units dispute who funds them, and no senior leader owns the program's direction. The program manager is asked to restart momentum. What should the program manager do FIRST?
options: Secure an executive sponsor to own direction and funding
Launch several more pilots across business units to build momentum
Hire an outside consulting firm to run the whole AI program end to end
Have IT rank the pilots by technical difficulty
questions.explanation: AWS's guidance on setting up an AI center of excellence says the foundational step is securing sponsorship from senior leadership to champion AI initiatives. Without a sponsor, funding disputes between business units have no one to resolve them.
whyWrong: More pilots add to the funding dispute without resolving it.
Outsourcing does not give the program a senior internal owner.
Technical difficulty does not settle who funds or directs the work.

questions.stem: A logistics firm's CEO sponsors the AI program and has set clear goals. Yet adoption in the regional depots is slow, and depot staff say they trust advice from colleagues more than messages from headquarters. The program director wants to sustain momentum across the depots. Which action is MOST effective?
options: Set mandatory usage targets with penalties for each depot
Identify AI champions in each depot to lead local efforts
Have the central team take over AI work in the depots
Wait for adoption to rise on its own as the AI tools improve
questions.explanation: AWS's maturity model lists identifying AI champions within the organization to lead the exploration of AI opportunities. Champions inside each depot carry the sponsor's goals to peers who already trust them.
whyWrong: Mandates push usage without building the peer trust the depots lack.
Central takeover removes the local ownership that spreads adoption.
Waiting leaves the trust gap untouched.

questions.stem: A hospital is forming a small squad to run a generative AI pilot that drafts patient discharge summaries. The CIO wants the squad to follow AWS guidance for cross-functional generative AI squads, so it can later grow into a center of excellence. Which members should the squad include? (Choose three.)
options: A marketing lead to plan launch publicity
The AI vendor's sales team as squad leads
Clinical leaders who own the discharge workflow
Security and governance stakeholders
Only IT engineers, to keep the squad small and fast
Generative AI specialists to lead experimentation
questions.explanation: AWS says squads should include IT representatives, business representatives, security and governance stakeholders, and generative AI experts who lead experimentation. Such a squad becomes the foundation for a formal center of excellence.
whyWrong: Publicity is not one of the roles a pilot squad needs.
A vendor sales team is not one of the roles AWS lists.
An IT-only squad lacks the business, security and governance voices AWS lists.

questions.stem: A bank has four generative AI applications in production, each run by a mix of business, IT, legal and compliance staff. After a prompt change caused wrong answers for a day, every team said another group had approved it. The COO wants this fixed before more applications launch. What should the COO put in place?
options: Approval by the model vendor for prompt and model changes
Sign-off by the CEO on each change before it goes live
A signed-off RACI with one accountable owner per change
Joint accountability shared equally by the four teams
questions.explanation: AWS's Launch level calls for signing off a first version of a RACI matrix for generative AI operations and defining roles and operational responsibilities for cross-functional AI teams. A RACI names who is responsible and who is accountable, so changes no longer fall between teams.
whyWrong: The vendor cannot own the bank's operational decisions.
Routing every change to the CEO creates a bottleneck without clarifying roles.
Shared accountability is how the change fell between teams.

questions.stem: A bank plans to pilot AI agents in back-office operations. Rumors of layoffs are spreading, and some staff have quietly stopped cooperating with the pilot team. The operations head has not yet said anything about how roles will change. What should the operations head do?
options: Stay quiet until the pilot proves results, then announce plans
Brief managers, keeping frontline staff out of it for now
Send one memo promising that no jobs will change
Share openly what will change, when, and the upskilling plan
questions.explanation: AWS advises leaders to be transparent about upskilling and about concerns over job displacement. Being open about what changes, when, and what it means for roles builds the trust adoption needs, while silence lets rumors fill the gap.
whyWrong: Silence lets the rumors keep shaping how staff see the pilot.
Leaving frontline staff out keeps them uninformed and resistant.
A blanket promise may prove false and destroy trust later.

questions.stem: At an insurer, underwriters rarely propose AI experiments. In interviews, they say earlier innovation projects that failed hurt the careers of the people who led them. The chief underwriting officer wants more bottom-up ideas for AI. Which leadership intervention addresses the barrier MOST directly?
options: Back small experiments and treat shutdowns as learning
Require a full business case before any experiment starts
Hire an outside AI team so underwriters avoid the risk
Require each underwriter to launch one AI project this year
questions.explanation: The barrier is fear of failure. AWS advises leaders to accept and embrace experimentation: run small experiments, measure the results, then scale what works or cost-effectively shut down what does not. That makes trying something safe.
whyWrong: A heavy business case raises the cost of trying.
Outsourcing confirms that experimenting is too risky for staff.
A mandate adds pressure without removing the fear.

questions.stem: A manufacturer's leadership plans to hire a small elite AI team that will work apart from the rest of the company. Experienced process engineers see the plan as a sign they will be replaced, and resistance to the AI program is growing. Which approach would BEST reduce the resistance?
options: Keep the elite team separate from engineering to protect its pace
Upskill existing engineers rather than rely on an elite team
Pay bonuses to engineers who adopt AI tools first
Delay the program until the resistance fades on its own
questions.explanation: AWS advises upskilling the whole organization rather than making AI knowledge the domain of an elite new team. Training existing staff builds talent that knows the business and eases the fear of people worried about their jobs.
whyWrong: Separation feeds the engineers' fear of being replaced.
Bonuses for early adopters divide staff without easing fear.
Resistance rooted in job fear does not fade without action.

questions.stem: A retail chain wants employees from store floors to the executive team to understand basic AI terms, set aside common myths and spot where AI could help their own work. Today, most staff treat AI as a mystery left to IT. Which workforce development approach fits this goal BEST?
options: A weekend hackathon for the central data science team
An all-staff demo day of the newest AI tools
A basic AI literacy course offered to all staff
Advanced certification courses for the platform engineers
questions.explanation: AWS stresses education from the C-suite down, helping stakeholders understand AI terms so that mystery is replaced with understanding. A literacy course for everyone does that, while a tools demo, a specialist hackathon or engineer certification does not.
whyWrong: A data science hackathon reaches specialists, not the whole workforce.
A product demo shows tools but does not build understanding of terms or myths.
Engineer certification builds specialist skills, not broad literacy.

questions.stem: A software company's chief people officer has two goals for the coming year. First, get people in every department building with AI themselves and generating new ideas. Second, make sure staff use AI within the company's agreed safe limits. Which approaches match these goals? (Choose two.)
options: Internal hackathons open to all teams in the company
A one-time executive keynote on the latest AI industry trends
Training sessions on the company's responsible AI guidelines
Limiting AI tools to the data science team for now
Outsourcing AI projects to a specialist vendor
questions.explanation: AWS's maturity model lists organizing internal hackathons to encourage experimentation and foster innovation. It also lists internal training sessions and developing guidelines for responsible AI use. Hackathons build hands-on ideas, and training builds responsible use.
whyWrong: A single talk raises awareness but builds no hands-on skill.
Restricting tools blocks the experimentation the goal calls for.
Outsourcing builds no internal skills or habits.

questions.stem: An insurer is introducing AI that drafts claim decisions from submitted documents. Claims adjusters currently spend most of their day keying data into forms. The claims VP must redesign the adjuster role so the company gains from the AI. Which redesign is MOST appropriate?
options: Remove adjusters and let the AI finalize all claim decisions
Keep adjusters keying data alongside the AI as a backup
Have adjusters spot-check a random sample of decisions monthly
Move adjusters to reviewing AI drafts and complex claims
questions.explanation: AWS describes individual contributors spending less time on routine tasks and more time solving problems, including checking AI outputs for accuracy. Reviewing drafts and handling complex claims puts adjusters' judgment where it adds the most.
whyWrong: Removing people drops the checking that AI output needs.
Duplicating the AI's work throws away the gain.
Monthly sampling leaves most AI drafts and complex claims without a person's judgment.

questions.stem: A regional sales manager's team now uses AI to produce routine forecasts and account summaries that the manager used to check line by line. The manager asks HR how the role should change. According to AWS guidance on workforce changes for AI, how should the manager's role evolve?
options: Toward mentoring staff and checking AI output quality
Toward checking each AI forecast line by line as before
Toward building and tuning the forecasting model personally
Toward a smaller role, with the AI replacing management
questions.explanation: AWS says managers need to evolve from traditional oversight to mentorship and quality assurance, validating that AI output meets quality standards while developing their people. Line-by-line checking or model building misses that shift.
whyWrong: Line-by-line review keeps the old task-oversight role.
Model tuning is a builder task outside the manager's role.
AWS describes the manager role changing, not being replaced.

questions.stem: A logistics firm's three AI pilots have met their success metrics, and business units are asking to use the tools every day. The pilots still run on a test setup with no on-call staff or formal approvals. The steering group follows the envision, experiment, launch, scale progression. What should the firm do next?
options: Run more pilots until each idea on the list has been tested
Put the proven pilots into governed, monitored production
Build a self-service AI platform for other departments
Return to awareness workshops to find better use cases
questions.explanation: The firm has completed Experiment, with pilots that validated business value. AWS's path to the next level is production-grade infrastructure, governance, observability and operational support, so the solutions are stable and reliable. A self-service platform belongs to Scale, and more pilots or workshops keep the firm at earlier levels.
whyWrong: More pilots keep the firm at Experiment after value is proven.
Self-service platforms belong to Scale, after production use is established.
Going back to Envision discards pilots that already met their metrics.

questions.stem: A retailer has five generative AI applications in production with governance, monitoring and support teams in place. Now twelve departments want their own applications, and the central team builds each one by hand, so the queue keeps growing. Using the envision, experiment, launch, scale progression, what should the AI program lead prioritize next?
options: Pause new requests until the five live apps are perfected
Let each department buy and run its own AI tools
Package reusable components into a self-service platform
Hire more engineers to keep building each app by hand
questions.explanation: The retailer is at Launch. AWS's strategy for reaching Scale is to identify reusable patterns and components and turn the platform into a self-service internal platform with standardized tools, workflows and governance. Pausing, hand-building or letting departments go separate ways does not scale with governance.
whyWrong: Pausing holds the retailer at Launch while demand grows.
Going separate ways loses the standard patterns and governance that Scale needs.
Hand-building each app does not scale and repeats the same work.

questions.stem: A bank's new chief data officer must show AI value within six months to a skeptical board. Two proposals are on the table: a three-year enterprise AI transformation, or a set of smaller projects. The chief data officer also wants a base for later expansion. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Start the full three-year transformation to show the board real ambition
Pick the use case that uses the most advanced technology
Wait until an enterprise AI platform is fully built
Begin with a feasible, high-impact use case with early results
questions.explanation: CAF-AI says starting somewhere is crucial and small wins drive faith in the organization, helping people see where else AI could help. It recommends a layered portfolio where lower layers enable upper ones, so early wins become a base for expansion.
whyWrong: A three-year program shows no value inside the board's window.
Novel technology is not the same as business impact.
Waiting for a full platform delays any proof of value.

questions.stem: A consumer goods company built a generative AI tool that searches and summarizes research documents for its product team, and it has shown clear value. Legal, audit and sales teams now ask for something similar. The AI program lead must decide how to expand. Which approach is BEST?
options: Reuse the proven capability only where teams show clear value
Build a separate tool for each department from scratch
Roll it out to each department at once, whether or not they need it
Keep it in the product team until it is perfect
questions.explanation: AWS advises identifying capabilities with broad applicability and reusing them across business units at relatively low marginal cost. It also cautions against replication as an end in itself, letting tangible value guide scaling decisions.
whyWrong: Rebuilding from scratch treats each case as a costly one-off.
Replicating without regard to value is what AWS warns against.
Waiting for perfection delays proven value to other teams.

questions.stem: A manufacturer set up an AI center of excellence two years ago. It reports to an infrastructure director three levels below the C-suite and is measured on research output. It has produced impressive prototypes, but business units say none solve their problems. What should the chief strategy officer change?
options: Increase the center's headcount to produce more prototypes
Align its goals and reporting line with business leaders
Disband the center and let each unit hire its own scientists
Give the center a bigger research budget and more autonomy
questions.explanation: CAF-AI says a center of excellence should have short paths to the C-suite and incentives aligned with strategy, business and customers. It warns that a common mistake is evolving AI units that do not deliver on business value.
whyWrong: More prototypes repeat the problem at greater cost.
Disbanding swings to the other extreme and loses shared expertise.
More autonomy widens the distance from business needs.

questions.stem: An insurer is writing the charter for a new AI center of excellence. The executive team has four draft statements of what the center should do. The goal is a center that helps business units scale AI while keeping standards consistent. Which charter statement BEST reflects AWS guidance?
options: Build and run the AI applications for each business unit centrally
Approve or reject AI ideas without input from business units
Guide units with best practices and shared technical capabilities
Focus on research and leave adoption entirely to business units
questions.explanation: AWS says an AI center of excellence should offer guidance, best practices and technical capabilities, and engage regularly with business units to find opportunities while maintaining governance and quality standards. Running everything centrally, or deciding without business units, works against that engagement.
whyWrong: Running everything centrally leaves business units without their own capability.
Deciding without business units cuts off the engagement AWS calls for.
Research with no link to adoption delivers little business value.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, an HR assistant's ROI is still the single figure calculated in the launch business case. Since then, usage has dropped in two regions and token costs have risen as a new feature rolled out. The HR director wants to know whether the assistant still earns its keep. What should the program adopt?
options: Recalculate ROI once a year at the annual budget review
A single user survey at the end of the year
Monitor latency and error rates as the main health signals
A live dashboard tracking costs against business value
questions.explanation: AWS says ROI cannot be a static calculation performed at launch. It must be tracked continuously on a dashboard that combines financial metrics, such as cost per interaction, with value metrics such as hours saved and satisfaction.
whyWrong: An annual check is too slow to catch changing costs and usage.
A single survey misses cost and changing usage.
Technical metrics alone do not show business value.

questions.stem: A retailer's customer chatbot has grown less accurate as the product range changed. Monitoring flags the drop and customers leave negative ratings, but the reports go to a shared inbox and no one acts on them. The digital director wants to protect long-term value. What should the director put in place?
options: Feed monitoring and ratings into regular improvements
Add more metrics to the monitoring dashboard
Freeze the chatbot so its answers stop changing over time
Switch to the newest model available each quarter
questions.explanation: AWS treats a production AI application as a living system whose value can degrade through drift and shifting user expectations. It calls for monitoring performance, gathering feedback and driving iterative improvements, which means signals must lead to action.
whyWrong: More metrics add signals no one acts on.
Freezing does not fix answers already falling behind the product range.
A new model does not close the loop between feedback and fixes.

questions.stem: A bank's proof of concept that drafts loan-decision letters impressed executives, and the sponsor wants it in production next month. The risk officer lists what must be in place before go-live, drawing on the Launch level of the AWS generative AI maturity model. Which items belong on the list? (Choose three.)
options: Monitoring and alerts for model performance and guardrails
A larger and newer model than the one used in the proof of concept
Operations and support teams with clear escalation paths
A press release announcing the launch to customers
Approved risk, governance, and responsible AI policies
Expansion plans for the other departments
questions.explanation: AWS's Launch level calls for risk, governance and responsible AI policies, operational and support teams with tiered support and escalation paths, and monitoring of model performance and guardrail violations with alerts. A bigger model or publicity does not make a pilot production-ready.
whyWrong: Model size is not a readiness requirement.
Publicity is not an operational or governance requirement.
Expansion belongs to Scale, after production proves out.

questions.stem: A logistics company's AI routing assistant has passed load, security and compliance testing and gone live. The project manager proposes closing the project, releasing the team and ending the budget line, since development is finished. How should the business owner view the move to production?
options: As the end of the project, with the budget line closed
As the start of ongoing ownership of its results
As handover to a support desk that fixes reported faults
As the point to shift the team to the next pilot
questions.explanation: AWS says preproduction is for hardening, testing and derisking, and that entering production is not a project conclusion. The application must be managed as a living system that keeps proving its worth, because its performance can degrade over time.
whyWrong: Closing out at launch leaves no one managing value or drift.
Fixing reported faults is not managing value, which can degrade unnoticed.
Moving all effort away leaves the live system unmanaged.

questions.stem: A retailer is scaling a generative AI shopping assistant from one region to twenty over the next year. The COO wants a short set of factors reviewed monthly to protect business continuity and performance as volume grows. Which factors should the COO track? (Choose two.)
options: Infrastructure and API cost efficiency as usage rises
Headcount of the central AI team
Programming language used to build the assistant
Latency, uptime, and SLA adherence as traffic grows
Number of prompts employees write each day across the stores
questions.explanation: AWS's guidance on monitoring production generative AI lists latency, throughput, uptime and SLA adherence, resource use and cost efficiency as application and system health metrics. These show whether growth is straining service or budget.
whyWrong: Team size does not show whether the service holds up at scale.
The build language says nothing about performance at scale.
Prompt counts measure activity, not service health or cost.

questions.stem: A telecom has scaled its GenAI support assistant from one product line to nine over six months. Dashboards show response speed, uptime and cost per request within targets. Yet escalations to human agents are rising in the newest product lines, where catalog details change often. Which factor should the operations head add to the monthly scaling review?
options: Server memory and GPU use in each region
Number of active users in each product line
Answer accuracy and drift by product line
Response speed during evening peak hours
questions.explanation: AWS's production monitoring guidance adds a model and AI quality pillar to system health, covering accuracy and relevance, hallucination rates and drift caused by changing inputs. Fast, cheap and available answers can still be wrong as content changes across a growing footprint.
whyWrong: Resource use is a system-health metric, and system health is already on target.
User counts show adoption, not whether the answers are still right.
Speed is already within target and does not explain wrong answers.
